What We Are Bound To Lose in an Optimized Future

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1089 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.
  • We look back at the year, count our achievements, contemplate our disappointments, and begin constructing a better version of ourselves for January.
  • This possibility deserves attention as we enter another year of accelerating algorithmic assistance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

December invites a peculiar ritual. We look back at the year, count our achievements, contemplate our disappointments, and begin constructing a better version of ourselves for January. In 2026, artificial intelligence became an increasingly available accomplice in this exercise. It can summarize our accomplishments, identify inefficiencies, suggest resolutions, and construct an impressively optimized roadmap for 2027. Yet imagine reviewing your year differently. Instead of asking what went according to blueprint, consider what happened because it didn't. The conversation you never intended to have. The problem that refused to disappear. The project that demanded more than you thought you could give. Perhaps the moments that changed you most were precisely those that resisted optimization.

This possibility deserves attention as we enter another year of accelerating algorithmic assistance. We have become extraordinarily good at eliminating inconvenience, yet psychological flourishing may depend partly on experiences that cannot be anticipated, accelerated, or outsourced. The interplay between friction and flow offers a way to understand why.

We generally prefer ease, but our relationship with effort is more complicated than this preference suggests. A 2024 meta-analysis in Psychological Bulletin confirmed that mental effort is commonly experienced as unpleasant. Yet research published in Cognition in 2025, drawing on six studies involving 2,883 participants, found that exerting effort can increase an activity's perceived meaningfulness. One experiment compared writing with and without ChatGPT assistance. Greater effort contributed to meaning only up to a point. Still, the findings illuminate something that efficiency calculations routinely overlook. We may dislike the difficulty of an experience while valuing what that difficulty allows us to become. This paradox helps explain why flow, the state of intense absorption described by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, cannot simply be manufactured by making everything easier.

According to recent reports, A meta-analysis examining the relationship between challenge and skill found that their balance contributes significantly to flow, alongside clear goals and a sense of control. More recent research in Communications Psychology emphasizes autonomy and the personal significance of an activity. Flow emerges through engagement with something sufficiently demanding to absorb us, yet manageable enough to sustain participation. The pianist needs a piece that stretches her abilities; the writer needs an idea that refuses to settle into easy sentences. Friction provides the resistance through which skill becomes experience, and experience becomes satisfaction.

Now consider an algorithmic environment increasingly designed to anticipate our desires and remove obstacles before we encounter them. Recommendations narrow our search; predictive systems streamline our choices, and generative AI can produce results without requiring us to navigate the uncertainties of creation. Such assistance can be enormously beneficial, particularly when it relieves unnecessary burdens. Yet when friction disappears indiscriminately, we risk losing opportunities for the very engagement that makes flow possible. A life engineered for effortless outcomes might become strangely impoverished in the experiences through which we develop competence, confidence, and curiosity. This remains a psychological risk rather than an established destiny, but it raises an essential question: Are we optimizing the quality of our experiences, or merely the speed with which we move through them?

In a recent development, research suggests that our conventional understanding of a good life may itself be incomplete. Some consider psychological richness a dimension of well-being alongside happiness and meaning. A related 2025 review in Trends in Cognitive Sciences describes psychologically rich lives as those containing diverse, interesting, and perspective-changing experiences. To be clear, such experiences are not uniformly pleasant. An unfamiliar place, a challenging encounter, or an unexpected reversal may enlarge our understanding precisely because it disrupts familiar assumptions. This opens an interesting perspective on December's customary stocktaking.

In a recent development, the experiences that made 2026 psychologically rich may be poorly represented by our conventional measures of success. A friendship deepened through disagreement, an unexpected professional change, or an abandoned plan that opened an unforeseen possibility might have contributed more to personal development than another efficiently completed task. Of course, hardship is not inherently beneficial. Financial insecurity, discrimination, illness, and exhausting administrative obstacles can diminish well-being and restrict agency. The distinction worth preserving is between friction that erodes our ability to flourish and friction that invites us to exercise it.

It has been revealed that the approaching latest year makes this distinction painfully relevant. Research on the fresh start effect shows that temporal landmarks, including the beginning of a new year, can motivate humans to pursue aspirations. Perhaps we could use this psychological opening differently in December 2026? Rather than designing another year around the elimination of effort, we might ask which forms of friction deserve a place in our lives. Which difficulties strengthen our abilities? Which uncertainties invite discovery? Which activities would lose their meaning if someone—or something—completed them for us?

In a recent development, the challenge is to choose meaningful friction deliberately, without turning everyday life into an obstacle course. BLISS offers five practical ways to cultivate that judgment.

According to recent reports, B — Begin before borrowing. Give your own imagination an opportunity to work before requesting an algorithmic solution.

According to recent reports, L — Let learning take time. Preserve activities in which gradual improvement brings satisfaction, even when shortcuts are readily available.

According to recent reports, I — Invite the unfamiliar. Explore beyond personalized recommendations; seek perspectives and experiences that might challenge established preferences.

S — Stay with the struggle. When a difficulty is productive, resist the urge to eliminate it immediately. Allow yourself the satisfaction of finding a way through.

According to recent reports, S — Save space for surprise. Leave some time unplanned, some questions unanswered, and some possibilities unexplored until they present themselves.

We can welcome intelligent technologies that reduce unnecessary suffering while protecting the experiences that develop natural intelligence. An increasingly capable algorithmic future need not become a frictionless one, provided we retain the freedom and capacity to choose where human effort matters. As 2026 ends, perhaps the most meaningful resolution for 2027 is not to become more efficient, organized, or productive. It is to become more attentive to what makes life worth living. The winding path through unfamiliar territory may take longer, demand more, and occasionally lead somewhere unexpected. Yet it may also reveal capacities and possibilities that a perfectly optimized route would never allow us to discover.

Industry observers note that we need friction to find flow. And sometimes, the detour is the destination.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I missed a deadline last week. The piece you’re reading was supposed to be filed before I headed out on a long weekend to Italy for my wife’s birthday.

Sources indicate that the main problem was I simply ran out of time to write the piece. An urgent stakeholder ask out of the blue, a couple of unanticipated work fire drills, and a long-standing evening social commitment earlier in the week made for a perfect storm, and something had to give.

The other problem and consequence was that I carried a chunk of guilt into the break.

It caught up with me at 6 am on the first morning, when I found myself drafting this column in my head. I should have been dozing peacefully. I continued to ruminate on my lengthy to-do list at work deep into day one as we headed from Venice into the Dolomites. My body was in Italy, but my brain was clearly still at my desk.

Recent findings suggest that switching off, particularly from work, is hard for most of us, and especially in an age of ubiquitous screens and wall-to-wall information competing for our attention. For me, that always-on reality plays a major role in the difficulties I have disconnecting from the daily grind.

It has been revealed that I’m fortunate to love my job, and if I’m candid, I probably take a little too much of my identity from it. I hold on tight, and the phone in my pocket is an ever-present enabler.

In a recent development, A meme that has stuck with me over the years goes something along the lines of being an adult is staring at medium screens all day only to come home and stare at a little screen while a massive screen is on in the background. The irony is not lost on me that I came across this rather withering take on modern life while scrolling on mentioned little screen.

Regardless of the role the screen plays, psychologists who study employee well-being describe what I was missing for the early part of the weekend as “psychological detachment.” A state where you are genuinely able to not think about work while away from it. The science suggests it’s an important thing to work on.

A 2025 meta-analysis of 32 studies found that vacationing has a strong effect on well-being, and that the effect lasts longer than earlier research suggested. A second, smaller analysis of eight studies points to detaching from work, along with physical activity, as among the most helpful things to do while you’re off. In another study that tracked teachers during a two-week break, exhaustion, anxiety, and low mood all declined, while those who kept ruminating about work recovered less.

Sources indicate that whatever the science claims, I know that for me the act of stepping away from work and being disciplined about not checking back in while I’m away is critical for my mental health and for staving off burnout. Getting out in nature and hiking or cycling or swimming keeps me present. It resets and recharges my batteries, and it tops up my creativity in a way that I find benefits what I am then able to bring back to the office.

Industry observers note that sure enough, as we drove deeper into the mountains on a crisp, blue-sky day, I could feel the golden autumnal hues and majestic rock formations drawing me in, closer to an elemental feeling of calm and happiness. That sense of equilibrium stayed with me all weekend, and while I’d be lying if I stated my mind didn’t occasionally drift to my desk, it was fleeting, with the knowledge that all the things would be waiting for me when I got back. Just like this piece was.

It has been revealed that with Thanksgiving on the horizon, and the holidays coming thick and fast thereafter, I’ll leave you with this bit of hard-earned advice: if your job is deeply entwined with your life and part of who you are, as mine is, time away can sometimes feel like a small act of disloyalty. It isn’t. In fact, it’s probably the most vital thing you can do to remain faithful to your work ethic, and to yourself.

In a recent development, and if you’ll be working over the holidays, or you’re not working right now, or you don’t have the benefit of someone on hand to carry some of the load for you (shout out to all the Grannies out there), or your vacation looks very different from mine, that’s all okay. Find the pockets where and when you can: an evening, a walk, an hour in front of a screen, or better yet a book, and let work wait. Above all else, be kind to yourself. That’s how you really give yourself a break.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a break from tradition, the park rangers at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska have awarded one of their 2026 Anan Bear Awards to a completely different animal species.
  • “This little mink was a frequent visitor at the trailhead and the beach in Anan,” the rangers write.
  • Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the annual Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears (and a lucky mink) spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a break from tradition, the park rangers at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska have awarded one of their 2026 Anan Bear Awards to a completely different animal species. For its tenacity in finding food, a small mink (Neogale vison)  walking around Anan Creek wins the On a Mission Award.

“This little mink was a frequent visitor at the trailhead and the beach in Anan,” the rangers write. “It seemed unconcerned by nearby humans, completely focused on the small crabs and other nibbles it could get ahold of. It was on a mission to eat!”.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the annual Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears (and a lucky mink) spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area also includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

It has been revealed that according to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears (Ursus americanus) and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish and survive the long winter ahead. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own antics and quirks.

In addition to the bears and mink, numerous other animals call Tongass home. Bald eagles (Haliaeetus leucocephalus), the Alexander Archipelago wolf (Canis lupus ligoni), and the Sitka black-tailed deer (Odocoileus hemionus sitkensis). Importantly, all five of North America’s Pacific salmon species are found within the forest—Chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha), coho (Oncorhynchus kisutch), pink (Oncorhynchus gorbuscha), sockeye  (Oncorhynchus nerka), and chum (Oncorhynchus keta). These five fish species help feed the bears and other mammals and birds who gather here.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behavior.

#156737. Two tech companies tried to reinvent the e-bike. Why DJI’s Amflow soared while Rivian’s ALSO floundered

Two tech companies tried to reinvent the e-bike. Why DJI’s Amflow soared while Rivian’s ALSO floundered

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two of the most interesting new electric bicycle companies in the world made headlines on the same day last week, and for two very different reasons.
  • In a recent development, amflow, the electric bicycle brand that emerged from the same engineering ecosystem responsible for DJI’s revolutionary Avinox drive system, just debuted its first commuter e-bike to widespread acclaim.
  • Both companies set out to build something arguably similar: a premium, high-performance electric bicycle that uses sophisticated technology to make riding easier, more enjoyable, and more practical.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two of the most interesting new electric bicycle companies in the world made headlines on the same day last week, and for two very different reasons.

In a recent development, amflow, the electric bicycle brand that emerged from the same engineering ecosystem responsible for DJI’s revolutionary Avinox drive system, just debuted its first commuter e-bike to widespread acclaim. Meanwhile, ALSO, the high-tech electric bicycle startup spun out of Rivian, unveiled that it was halting deliveries of its futuristic TM-B electric bicycle amid mounting software problems.

Both companies set out to build something arguably similar: a premium, high-performance electric bicycle that uses sophisticated technology to make riding easier, more enjoyable, and more practical. Both have deep engineering roots and were incubated by successful technology companies. And both have developed impressive proprietary systems that set their bikes apart from the competition.

But their dramatically different launches offer an interesting lesson about the difference between innovation and execution, and which has proven to be more successful in the real world.

Amflow’s story actually begins before the brand launched its first electric mountain bike.

Sources indicate that DJI, the Chinese drone giant, had spent years perfecting the art of building small, lightweight, powerful electric motors, sophisticated electronic controllers, and advanced battery management systems. Those are all technologies that translate remarkably well to electric bicycles, even if the applications are quite different.

According to recent reports, that expertise helped give rise to the Avinox e-bike drive system, which quickly earned a reputation as one of the most impressive electric bicycle drivetrains on the market. The mid-drive motor and control system rapidly ate away at the huge market share long held by Bosch and other leaders.

The motors offered an almost ridiculous amount of power in a lightweight package, paired with sophisticated sensors and software that delivered smooth, natural-feeling pedal assistance. The system was also designed as a tightly integrated ecosystem, with displays, controllers, batteries, and motors working together.

Amflow’s first electric mountain bikes demonstrated just how well that technology could work in the real world.

And now, with the launch of the latest Amflow UE commuter series, the company is taking that proven technology and applying it to an entirely different kind of riding.

The latest bikes bring Avinox’s powerful pedal assistance and intelligent electronic controls to a more practical urban platform, adding commuter-focused features designed to make everyday riding more convenient.

There’s plenty of proprietary technology here, but perhaps the most important thing about Amflow’s approach is what the manufacturer didn’t reinvent.

The bikes still fundamentally work like bicycles.

You pedal, a conventional mechanical drivetrain transfers that power to the rear wheel, and an electric motor provides assistance. It’s the same basic arrangement that has worked on electric bicycles for decades, just refined with much more advanced engineering.

Amflow didn’t need to fundamentally change the bicycle to make it feel futuristic. Instead, the company focused on making the familiar bicycle experience better.

And while the new commuter models are still too fresh to judge their long-term reliability, early impressions have been overwhelmingly positive. That’s an encouraging start, especially considering the company’s already established reputation in the demanding electric mountain bike market.

ALSO, on the other hand, took a dramatically different approach.

The company emerged from Rivian, the American electric vehicle manufacturer known for its technologically advanced electric trucks and SUVs.

Like DJI, Rivian has extensive experience developing sophisticated electric drivetrains, battery systems, power electronics, and software. And like Amflow, ALSO wanted to bring that expertise to a fresh generation of electric bicycles.

But instead of using those technologies to improve a conventional bicycle, ALSO decided to rethink the entire machine.

The company’s TM-B electric bicycle uses a pedal-by-wire system, meaning the pedals aren’t mechanically connected to the rear wheel. Instead, pedaling turns a generator that sends data signals and power through an electronic system, while software determines how the rear motor responds.

Pedal-by-wire systems have some genuine potential advantages. They can eliminate traditional chains, belts, derailleurs, and other mechanical drivetrain components, which has helped land them on many unconventional e-bikes such as extremely long cargo e-bikes and truck-like electric bicycles that would otherwise require ridiculously long chain runs.

They can also allow engineers to completely customize the relationship between pedaling effort and motor response, creating riding experiences that wouldn’t be possible with a conventional bicycle drivetrain.

In a recent development, but there’s a catch. When you replace a relatively simple mechanical system with a sophisticated electronic one, you’re also introducing a lot more opportunities for things to go wrong.

And unlike a conventional bicycle, where many drivetrain problems can be diagnosed and repaired with basic tools, a highly proprietary software-defined bicycle can become much more dependent on its manufacturer to keep it running.

Sources indicate that that’s not inherently a bad tradeoff. Modern electric cars have demonstrated that software-defined vehicles can offer tremendous benefits. But it puts enormous pressure on the manufacturer to get the hardware, software, and integration right.

Unfortunately, ALSO’s early rollout suggests that the company hasn’t quite managed that yet.

The contrast between the two companies became particularly striking last week.

Amflow unveiled its fresh commuter models, building on the reputation of its successful electric mountain bikes and earning enthusiastic early reviews.

ALSO, meanwhile, confirmed that it was pausing deliveries of its TM-B electric bicycle due to software-related complications. That’s on top of earlier delivery delays and reports of customers having to send their fresh ALSO TM-B bicycles back for repairs.

We’ve also previously reported on some unusual charging and discharging behavior with the TM-B, raising questions about how the bike’s sophisticated electronic systems were managing energy. Those concerns now look particularly relevant in light of the company’s latest announcement.

To be fair, we don’t know how widespread the problems are across ALSO’s delivered bicycles, and it’s entirely possible that the company will resolve these issues relatively quickly with updates on delivered bikes and reflashing software on bikes yet to be shipped.

Nor should we assume that Amflow’s new commuter bikes will be trouble-free simply because their initial reviews are positive. Long-term reliability is something that can only be established over time. But the difference in their respective releases is hard to ignore.

Both are examples of tech-focused startups attempting to reinvent the future of e-bikes. One company is expanding its lineup after successfully establishing its technology in the market. The other is struggling to get its first product consistently into customers’ hands.

And that brings us to what I think is the most interesting part of this story.

There’s a fundamental difference between developing impressive technology and successfully turning that technology into a dependable consumer product.

Both Amflow and ALSO have accomplished the first part.

The engineering behind the Avinox drive system is genuinely impressive, and the TM-B’s pedal-by-wire architecture is one of the more ambitious attempts to rethink the electric bicycle in recent years.

But Amflow appears to have taken a more measured approach to bringing that technology to consumers.

The tech giant first developed and refined a sophisticated electric bicycle drivetrain, proved it in the demanding electric mountain bike market, and then adapted it to commuter applications.

ALSO attempted something much more ambitious right out of the gate: launching an entirely latest bicycle architecture with numerous interdependent proprietary systems.

Recent findings suggest that neither approach is inherently wrong. In fact, if nobody ever attempted the latter, we’d probably miss out on some genuinely revolutionary products. But there’s a reason that so many successful technological innovations are evolutionary rather than revolutionary.

Sources indicate that sometimes the smartest engineering decision isn’t figuring out how to replace something that already works. It’s figuring out how to make it work better.

And there’s a certain irony in the fact that Amflow’s upcoming commuter bike looks relatively ordinary, yet appears to deliver an extraordinary riding experience.

ALSO’s TM-B, meanwhile, looks like something from the future, but its early ownership experience has been considerably less impressive.

I want to be clear that I’m not rooting for or against either company here.

Industry observers note that quite the opposite. Both ALSO and Amflow are working to accelerate the state of the industry. I’ve been fascinated by the TM-B since it was first unveiled, and I genuinely hope the company succeeds. And Amflow has taken the fresh perspective brought by its parent company, DJI, and turned it into real-world progress. The e-bike industry needs more innovation to help push everyone forward.

I love seeing companies take big swings in the electric bicycle industry, especially when they’re attempting something more interesting than slapping a bigger motor and battery onto an otherwise generic frame.

And I think pedal-by-wire technology has real potential. The ability to electronically control the relationship between pedaling and propulsion opens up fascinating possibilities, even if it also introduces upcoming challenges.

According to recent reports, I should also mention that I have not personally ridden either of these bikes, and thus this is analysis from the sidelines. The Amflow UE Carbon was only unveiled a few days ago, though I’ve got one on the way and am excited to begin testing it soon and to report back here on the experience. As for ALSO, the bike was unveiled a year ago, and I was slated to be at the launch for test riding, but barely an hour after I posted an exclusive article revealing that ALSO had accidentally leaked its own images of its yet-to-be-unveiled bike on its website, I received an email uninviting me to the upcoming event and test ride.

So keep in mind that all of this is being said as an analyst with nearly two decades in the e-bike industry and hundreds of different e-bikes under my belt, not from personal experience with either bike model.

Sources indicate that but as someone who spends an enormous amount of time riding, testing, and working on electric bicycles, I also appreciate the value of simplicity. A bicycle is an inherently elegant machine. It’s lightweight, efficient, relatively easy to maintain, and remarkably dependable considering how few components it needs to function.

It has been revealed that electric assistance has already made that machine dramatically more useful for millions of people. The question is how much more complexity we should introduce in pursuit of further improvements.

Amflow seems to be asking, “How can we use advanced technology to make riding a bicycle better?”.

ALSO seems to be asking, “What if we could completely rethink how a bicycle works?”.

It has been revealed that both are worthwhile questions, and I’m glad there are companies pursuing both answers. But right now, Amflow is demonstrating the advantages of building on a proven foundation, while ALSO is learning some painful lessons about the challenges of reinventing the wheel.

It's pretty clear that electric cars are much simpler than ICE cars, and I would argue this is an advantage. However, the same cannot be said for the ALSO bike. It's much more complicated than a normal bike, or even a normal e-bike. It seems like an answer in search of a problem.

And perhaps that’s the biggest takeaway from this tale of two high-tech e-bike startups.

The future of electric bicycles will undoubtedly involve more sophisticated motors, batteries, sensors, and software. But the companies that succeed won’t necessarily be the ones that pack the most technology into their bikes.

They’ll be the ones that figure out how to make all that technology work so seamlessly that riders barely have to think about it.

In a recent development, because at the end of the day, the best electric bicycle isn’t necessarily the one with the most advanced technology. It’s the one that makes you want to ride it every day – and actually lets you.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that at the debut of the redesigned Mercedes-Benz GLA, firm chairman Ola Källenius said, “The ICE [internal-combustion engine] world and the BEV [battery-electric vehicle] world have come together.” And that’s true: Apart from their grilles, the gas-engine GLA and the first-ever GLA EV are virtually indistinguishable from each other.
  • Electric-first is also the go-to-market strategy—at least in Europe.
  • See all results for new 2028 Mercedes-Benz GLA-Class EV for sale near 29405.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that at the debut of the redesigned Mercedes-Benz GLA, firm chairman Ola Källenius said, “The ICE [internal-combustion engine] world and the BEV [battery-electric vehicle] world have come together.” And that’s true: Apart from their grilles, the gas-engine GLA and the first-ever GLA EV are virtually indistinguishable from each other. Källenius described the design of the newly introduced GLA as “clearly electric-first,” so it’s perhaps appropriate that the EV version is the first one we’re driving.

Electric-first is also the go-to-market strategy—at least in Europe. It was to be in the U.S., too, but there’s been a reversal; we’re now slated to get the GLA hybrid first. Really, though, we won’t be getting either one for a while. We’re told to expect the gas-engine GLA sometime late next year, while the EV won’t arrive until the first half of 2028. Our recent drive of the electric GLA in Spain, therefore, was an extra-long-lead preview.

See all results for new 2028 Mercedes-Benz GLA-Class EV for sale near 29405.

We’d say that gives buyers plenty of time to warm up to the new styling, except that the look is not all that different from the current GLA. More substantial, maybe: The body is bigger, sitting astride a wheelbase that is stretched 2.4 inches. The new GLA is also longer, lower, and wider.

The GLA EV is also adorned with more three-pointed stars, though not to the extent of some other recent Mercedes products. Besides the illuminated logo on the flat-panel “grille,” there’s a large badge on the rear liftgate, and the motif also appears in the headlights and taillights. Opt for Sky Control for the standard glass roof panel, and 172 light-up stars appear on the glass, which is electronically dimmable in sections.

The dash is lifted straight from the GLA’s sedan sibling, the CLA. As in other Benz models, there’s an available Superscreen that adds a 14.0-inch passenger display to the standard 14.0-inch center touchscreen and 10.3-inch instrument screen. With it, virtually the entire dashboard is given over to digital real estate. Sadly, almost none of the space contains any physical switchgear, although at least we still get air vents that can be aimed by hand. Wireless smartphone mirroring is standard, but a wireless charging pad costs extra. The navigation uses Google Maps and optionally offers Benz’s augmented reality, an inset showing a forward-camera view with overlaid arrows indicating direction. Unfortunately, that inset appears on the left side of the touchscreen, where it’s obscured by the driver’s right hand on the wheel; you have to peer around to see it.

The on-screen climate controls are another ergonomic fail, as the touch points to change the temperature are tiny, and you have to open the climate menu to adjust the fan speed. You could ask for help from Benz’s digital assistant, which lurks within the screen, always listening. And there’s a camera trained on the driver, which can use facial recognition to automatically call up the driver’s profile and saved preferences. It can also take selfies! In a more worthwhile use of technology, buyers can purchase dash-cam functionality for the forward-facing camera.

See all results for fresh 2028 Mercedes-Benz GLA-Class EV for sale near 29405.

Beyond the digital, the interior features high-back front seats that are firmly padded and well shaped. The high center console makes for a somewhat confining feel up front, but its floating design creates a large open bay underneath for storage. The rear-seat area boasts a flat floor and is much roomier than in the CLA sedan. The cargo hold is 15 cubic feet, expandable to 49 cubes with the rear seatbacks folded. There’s also a frunk that’s about the size of a carry-on suitcase.

In a recent development, the powertrains mirror the CLA EV’s. There’s a single-motor GLA250+ that sends 268 horsepower to the rear wheels. The dual-motor GLA350 4Matic has all-wheel drive and 349 horses. Both employ a two-speed transmission on the rear axle for improved efficiency at highway speeds.

Recent findings suggest that the standard suspension has passive dampers, but the cars we drove had the optional adaptive dampers and rode on 20-inch wheels (18s are standard; 19s are also available). The smooth pavement of Barcelona and sunny coastal environs gave the dampers little to adapt to—any real assessment of the GLA’s ride quality will have to wait until we drive one on the meaner streets back home. However, the suspension acquitted itself well on our drive route’s long series of hillside curves. The GLA is composed but would be more confidence-inspiring if the steering weren’t so light and remote.

The GLA isn’t a hot hatch, though; it’s more of an urban runabout. In that context, the 268-hp GLA250+ is adequately peppy, even though Mercedes posits a rather languid 60-mph time of 7.2 seconds. We expect it to do better than that, as the CLA250+ we tested managed a 5.8-second result. The dual-motor GLA350 felt much more energetic, particularly outside of urban environs, where it swiftly passed dawdlers on two-lane roads and merged easily onto the freeway. For the GLA350, Mercedes claims a 5.3-second 60-mph time, but again that’s likely an undersell; testing a mechanically identical CLA350, we got 4.3 seconds. Even so, there are quicker EVs in this class, but one positive here is that even the higher-horsepower dual-motor version doesn’t feel like its output overwhelms its chassis—often an issue with high-horsepower EVs. Besides the standard drive modes of Eco, Comfort, Sport, and Individual, the dual-motor GLA adds a Terrain mode that optimizes the powertrain for loose surfaces; its camera system is able to stitch together a “transparent hood” view of what’s immediately in front of the car.

According to recent reports, when it comes time for slowing, there are three levels of liftoff regen (D, D+, and D-), as well as an Auto setting that varies the regen level based on info from the navigation system and the forward-facing cameras. Our preference is D-, which is essentially coasting, but D+ will please fans of one-pedal driving. We also tried the automated parking function, which was able to back into and out of a parallel-parking spot without trying our patience. It’s a digital add-on that’s purchased for a set time period; the same goes for the MBUX Entertainment package of multimedia streaming and app downloads.

Like the CLA EV sedan, the GLA is built on Benz’s MMA platform, with an 800-volt architecture and an 85-kWh battery. That architecture allows for speedy DC recharging, up to 320 kilowatts. Should you find a power source robust enough to reach that figure, Mercedes notes the GLA battery can go from 10 percent to 80 percent in 22 minutes. (In our testing of the CLA250+ with the same hardware, it went from 10 to 80 percent in just 21 minutes.) EPA range estimates for the GLA aren’t yet available, but the CLA offers a clue, and its impressive range figures run from 312 miles on the low end to as high as 374 miles.

Sources indicate that if the GLA ends up with numbers like those, it’ll look pretty good against the electric Mini Countryman, Genesis GV60, and Cadillac Optiq, and similar-ish to a Rivian R2. Those look to be the GLA EV’s prime competitors at a base-price guesstimate of around $50K. But the EV landscape could shift significantly by the time the GLA gets here. After all, a lot can happen between now and 2028.

If you've been thinking about getting into sim racing, Black Friday is a great opportunity to upgrade your setup without spending a fortune. The Logitech G923 Racing Wheel and Pedals, which we named ‘Best for Beginners’ in our Best Sim Racing Wheels roundup, is currently 29 percent off.

The G923 offers an approachable introduction to sim racing, with a leather-wrapped steering wheel, paddle shifters, and a three-pedal setup for even more real action. Logitech's Trueforce technology adds detailed vibrations that respond to in-game physics, making everything from cornering to changes in road surfaces feel more realistic. Unlike more expensive direct-drive setups, the G923 doesn't require a dedicated racing cockpit to get started. It's a practical choice for anyone looking to graduate from a controller to a proper steering wheel.

With GTA VI generating excitement around gaming upgrades, it's also worth checking out our guide to gaming gear for GTA VI. While the G923 isn't compatible with that game, it's an excellent addition for players interested in dedicated racing titles.

At $250, this beginner-friendly setup is a worthwhile Black Friday purchase for aspiring sim racers.

  • Alongside showing everything coming with this next revision, the developer also confirmed that 3.8 will go on for eight weeks, rather than the usual six.
  • The story in "Memories are the Prelude to Dreams" takes place after the final battle of Amphoreus, where Constance "The Dahlia" appears to deliver a twist: the Trailblazer's memories are scattered, with many parts missing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, hoYoverse just hosted a sizeable Honkai: Star Rail Special Program, revealing more than just the game’s next major revision. Version 3.8 was the big highlight, of course, with the new release arriving soon, on December 16-17 depending on your server region.

Alongside showing everything coming with this next revision, the developer also confirmed that 3.8 will go on for eight weeks, rather than the usual six. V3.8 is dubbed "Memories are the Prelude to Dreams", and it brings an end to the Amphoreus journey.

The story in "Memories are the Prelude to Dreams" takes place after the final battle of Amphoreus, where Constance "The Dahlia" appears to deliver a twist: the Trailblazer's memories are scattered, with many parts missing.

This final quest revolves around finding them in order to piece together the mystery, and involves a return to Penacony. This memory-hunting adventure is told from the perspective of Firefly, which will also explain how she entered the dreamscape initially and met the squad.

The new playable character is The Dahlia, whose power is linked to the the Remembrance path, which allows her to fabricate memories. Despite taking her powers from the Remembrance, The Dhalia actually follows the Path of Nihility in-game: she’s a 5-Star character who shines in teams dealing Break DMG.

The Dhalia can unleash a Gloomy Zone that causes Toughness Reduction inflicted by allies to trigger Super Break DMG, even before you break your enemies’ Weaknesses. The Dahlia can also invite one teammate to become her Dance Partner, which allows them (and her) to deal additional Super Break DMG each time they attack an enemy. If you trigger her Ultimate after picking a Dance Partner, she applies Type Weaknesses of both partners to enemies.

While The Dahlia is the only new character appearing in this final Amphoreus update, there'll be reruns aplenty, with an unusual third banner phase to make up for the extra long wait for 4.0. Appropriately for her role in the story, Firefly will make her return alongside The Dahlia in Phase 1, while Fugue and Lingsha will both have banner reruns in Phase 2, which is expected on January 7th. A bonus two-week-long Phase 3 will then begin on January 28th, seeing brief reappearances for popular returning characters Aglaea and Sunday, before things (presumably) go back to normal with the new annual update.

Something else to look forward to in 3.8 is The Chrysos Awoo Championship, which invites players to become chimera trainers and compete in team-based battles. The Remnants of Twilight event kicks off with the new patch, too, featuring its own set of challenges. However, HoYoverse have confirmed that there won't be an extra event during Phase 3 — but hopefully that'll give you some time to wrap up the last of the Amphoreus story content, which is longer than the previous four chapters put together.

Latest Update: What Darwin’s Bees Tell Us About Right and Wrong

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (965 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.
  • Industry observers note that evolutionary explanations of morality have been of scientific interest since at least Darwin.
  • This is why I’ve recently published an academic article on the topic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.

Industry observers note that evolutionary explanations of morality have been of scientific interest since at least Darwin. Proto-Darwinian explanations, however, have been around for much longer. The attempt to explain morality has a long tradition going back as far as ancient Greece.

This is why I’ve recently published an academic article on the topic.

Protagoras, in one of Plato’s dialogues, provides perhaps the first scientific explanation of morality as a set of norms and enforcement agencies, an invention of humanity to escape a Hobbesian state of nature. Couched in terms of a myth, we may treat this as a mere just-so story.

Sources indicate that much later, David Hume came astonishingly close to providing a Darwinian explanation of morality himself. Rainer Hegselmann and Oliver Will identify four key components of Hume’s account: a pre-societal human nature with confined generosity, the invention of artificial values to be reinforced and internalized through the approval and disapproval of others, a division of labor reaping the benefits of cooperation and trust, and the invention of central authorities that monitor, enforce, and eventually punish behavior.

These accounts, a mere story and myth in the case of Protagoras and an informal suggestion of a how-possibly explanation in the case of Hume, leave much to be desired, but they were nevertheless the best explanations available at the time.

Sources indicate that luckily, it did not take two millennia for the next advancement. Less than a century after Hume’s death, Darwin delivered the means for pushing the inquiry into human morality further, filling a gap Hume could only describe as nature.

In a recent development, darwin himself suggested that the origin of morality can be explained with his theory. He did not maintain that any social animal, if its intellectual faculties were to become as highly developed as ours, would acquire exactly the same moral sense. If, to take his extreme case, humans were reared under precisely the same conditions as hive-bees, our unmarried females would, like the worker-bees, “think it a sacred duty to kill their brothers.” Mothers would strive to kill their fertile daughters, and no one would think of interfering. Nevertheless, the bee, or any other social animal, would gain, as it appeared to Darwin, some feeling of right or wrong, or a conscience.

The thought is unsettling. What a creature feels to be right and wrong depends on the kind of creature it is and the conditions under which it lives.

According to recent reports, this, of course, is still “just” a how-possibly explanation, or, as critics like to call them, a just-so story. It should be clear, however, that from Protagoras over to Hume to Darwin, significant improvements in the explanation of morality have been made, with more and more gaps being closed. Explanations come in degrees, and this research program is providing better and better explanations.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, it took a while until informal evolutionary explanations resting on the good of the species were replaced with formal models from evolutionary game theory, showing that the origin of moral behavior is not much of a mystery after all. The philosopher Brian Skyrms was the first to apply evolutionary game theory to unpack Hume’s account in a formal manner, with others following in the creation of latest models and simulations.

These sets of models strengthen our confidence that morality could have evolved in a way envisioned by Hume and Darwin, providing considerable explanatory power, even though empirical work has, hitherto, been largely left out of the picture.

Sources indicate that modelers such as Skyrms simply continue an old philosophical school of thought with the modern tools of science, a move that ought to be encouraged. Even the work of moral philosophers in this Humean tradition has been very empirical and guided by science, trying to unpack the idea of morality being a mere artifact. It is a case in point for the division of labor between philosophers, modelers, and empirical researchers.

Sources indicate that akin to other primates, evolution equipped us with emotions and other cognitive machinery in order to solve interdependent decision problems. We do not know yet which of our moral attitudes are hard-wired and which are culturally acquired, but that is obviously no reason not to ask the question. Darwin’s bees tell us what kind of answer to expect: one that depends on the problems of living together that a species has to solve.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, bentley may not exactly be the first name in off-road performance, but the British luxury brand made its first moves toward that horizon with a surprise concept in January. Now, it looks like that Bentayga X concept might be headed for production in the near future.

Recent findings suggest that in an interview with Automotive News, CEO Frank-Steffen Walliser says that reaction to the Bentayga X was “really surprisingly positive.” When asked directly if the brand was considering building the concept as a production model, Walliser stated that “yes, we have this on the horizon. Time will tell us when it’s ready.”.

That is not quite a direct confirmation of production intends, but it is pretty much as close as an executive will get without directly announcing a new model. It’s also great news for buyers hoping to get their hands on a Bentayga with more off-road capability—an option that has never before been available in the company’s century-long history.

The concept shown in January added over two inches of ride height and nearly five inches of track width to the basic Bentayga Speed, bringing total ground clearance over 12 inches and total wading depth up to 21.6 inches. While we do not know how much of the concept would make its way into a theoretical production Bentayga X, it would be safe to assume that the final product would ride higher and sit wider than a typical Bentley SUV. All-terrain rubber and extra lighting elements, both seen on the concept, could also presumably make their way to the finished product.

Sources indicate that fred Smith's love of cars comes from his fascination with auto racing. Unfortunately, that passion led him to daily drive a high-mileage, first-year Porsche Panamera. He is still thinking about the last lap of the 2011 Indianapolis 500.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hailey Bieber is sharing her experience with premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), a condition she claims has fueled her growing interest in women’s health research.

The Rhode Beauty founder recently revealed a $5 million, three-year partnership with the Foundation for Women’s Health in an interview with Women’s Wear Daily (WWD).

“As a woman, I feel frustrated by the lack of research, the lack of awareness, the lack of certain conversation around it,” Bieber told WWD.

Industry observers note that motherhood has also shaped her perspective. Bieber welcomed her son, Jack Blues, with her husband, Justin Bieber, in 2024, describing the experience as a “really intense and special journey.”.

She also shared that she “struggled” with PMDD after giving birth, noting that there’s “not a lot of conversation or research around it.”.

“When we can identify with each other and have conversations relating to each other and talking about the things we’re dealing with and struggling with, I do think it makes it feel like less of a lonely journey,” Bieber said.

PMDD is a complexcondition that causes severe physical and psychological symptoms that typically occur in the days or weeks leading up to menstruation.

“What distinguishes PMDD from the more common PMS (premenstrual syndrome) is the severity of the symptoms and how significantly they can interfere with daily functioning,” Sari Eitches, MD, dual board certified physician and medical advisor to Terra Mare, told Healthline.

“Another defining feature is the timing: symptoms typically worsen in the week or two before a period, resolve within a few days after menstruation begins, and are minimal or absent during the rest of the cycle,” she said.

Eitches also noted that PMDD is a chronic condition that can affect women at any stage of their reproductive lives, from adolescence through perimenopause, as long as they are having menstrual cycles.

“It is caused by a sensitivity to cyclic hormonal and neurotransmitter fluctuations, so [it] can occur in anyone with a menstrual cycle, though stages of hormonal fluctuation- including postpartum, weaning breastfeeding, and perimenopause- can be a trigger,” she added.

According to research published in 2024, approximately 1.6% of women and girls meet the strict diagnostic criteria for PMDD, equivalent to an estimated 31 million people worldwide.

A higher percentage of 3.2% have a provisional diagnosis, meaning a healthcare professional may believe a person has PMDD, but symptoms have not been measured for a sustained amount of time to meet the criteria for a confirmed diagnosis.

Eitches said that women with a personal or family history of depression or anxiety may be more prone to developing PMDD, as are women with a family history of PMDD itself.

“PMDD is understood to be caused by a combination of heritable biological sensitivities and environmental triggers. These can include a history of trauma, chronic stress, and other chronic medical conditions,” she noted.

Eitches also stated that you should consider seeing a doctor if your symptoms are severe enough that they’re interfering with your ability to go to work or school, maintain your relationships, or participate in your life in the same way that you do during the other weeks of the month.

To diagnose PMDD, a healthcare professional will review your medical history and symptoms and may perform a physical exam. They will typically ask you to track your symptoms over at least two menstrual cycles.

A PMDD diagnosis generally requires at least five symptoms, including at least one mood-related symptom, that occur before menstruation, improve shortly after a period begins, and significantly interfere with daily life.

Treatment options for PMDD include prescription medications and over-the-counter treatments that may help relieve certain symptoms, such as:.

Eitches noted that cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can also help manage symptoms.

Lifestyle changes may also help manage PMDD symptoms, including practicing relaxation techniques, eating a balanced diet, limiting sugary and salty foods, and getting regular physical activity.

Eitches noted that getting enough high quality sleep and resting on a consistent schedule is also important.

“I also recommend focusing on a whole-foods-based diet, limiting added sugar and caffeine, and avoiding cigarette smoking,” she remarked.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, battlefield 6 is about to receive a upcoming patch. Version 1.1.3.0 is set to arrive tomorrow, December 9 to kick off the third and final phase of the game’s first season. Winter Offensive brings some holiday-themed new content to the game, but it’s not the most interesting part of the patch.

That honour goes to a couple of the high-level changes Battlefield Studios has included with the newly introduced patch, which range from a major pass on audio to a fix for a particularly annoying bug that’s been seemingly introduced with a recent patch.

According to recent reports, thew fresh content takes the form of a limited-time version of the game’s Empire State map, which covers it in snow and tweaks its layout slightly. To go along with that there are new limited-time modes for both multiplayer and Redsec’s Gauntlet. The event mode will be available in Conquest, and Domination.

The Ice Climbing Axe is the only new weapon in this drop. The battle pass gets a new Winter Offensive bonus path, just like we’ve seen with previous seasonal stages. This is how you unlock the axe, too.

Easily the most interesting change in this revision is the range of improvements to audio across the board. First, footstep audio received a substantial pass that should make it easier to hear enemy footsteps, easier to locate them, and across different surfaces.

In a recent development, some of the bugs that caused certain sounds to simply vanish have been fixed. This was especially prevalent in battle royale matches. BF Studios explained in the patch notes that it has adjusted memory priorities for in-game sounds in order to prioritise the most crucial ones. This is not the end of the road on audio, however, as the developer continues to work on making the soundscape more stable and reliable.

Some of those audio changes are the result of recent testing done in Battlefield Labs, which is also responsible for another exciting addition in this latest patch: improvements to hit registration.

While BF6 has had solid and stable netcode, certain situations would sometimes create uncertainty about how you died, and why certain actions seemingly failed to perform at that particular moment.

The focus in this update is to improve the reliability of how actions in close-quarter combat are translated, which includes firing before fully going into ADS, quick aim changes and more.

Speaking of close-range, the patch also brings another pass to soldier visibility to make it easier for enemies to stand out from the background. This is particularly relevant in areas with low contrast, or busy environments with lots of particle and visual effects.

1.1.3.0 also brings yet another set of weapon handling and gunplay tweaks, this time focusing on accuracy concerns with first shots. You can also expect more tweaks to attachment behaviour with regards to recoil.

It has been revealed that something else worth highlighting is that vehicle gameplay is getting several smaller tweaks that have to do with how they interact with the world, how their HUDs behave and more. Finally, your settings should no longer be reset after applying an upgrade. BF Studios claims there are still some instances where that might happen, but the issue should be fixed for the majority of players.

You can read the full change log on the Battlefield blog.

"You Don't Sound Autistic to Me"

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1241 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.
  • Autism Spectrum Disorder has historically been diagnosed with a full psychological assessment.
  • Industry observers note that for most neurotypicals, the IQ score is a good estimate of their ability to perform across multiple domains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

Autism Spectrum Disorder has historically been diagnosed with a full psychological assessment. This assessment includes observational tests and a full Intelligence Quotient (IQ) test. Autism is often easy to see on an IQ assessment because IQ isn’t just one number. It is an assessment of a person’s strengths and weaknesses across multiple domains. The IQ number we are used to seeing is a representation of the average of many different types of aptitudes and weaknesses. Verbal comprehension, fluid reasoning, processing speed, and visual-spatial abilities are all measured with an index score that is put together to form an overall IQ score. IQ itself is a measure of averages. 100 is the average IQ. 15 is the standard deviation of the mean, so if you have an IQ above 115, you are more intelligent than 84% of the general population, and if you have an IQ of 130, you are smarter than 98% of the population.

Industry observers note that for most neurotypicals, the IQ score is a good estimate of their ability to perform across multiple domains. It is rare for someone to have a verbal comprehension score in the 99th percentile and a working memory score in the 5th percentile. This is normal and is part of why, if you speak well, most neurotypicals assume you are intelligent across multiple domains. However, one of the hallmarks of autism that isn’t frequently discussed is what is known as a “spiky profile”. A spiky profile means that I frequently see clients with an overall IQ that is virtually meaningless because they will have verbal reasoning in the 5th percentile and be nonverbal, but have a fluid reasoning and visual spatial score in the 99th percentile, or vice versa.

Industry observers note that this spiky profile deeply impacts how the world and the public relate to autism and autistic people. Humans in general strongly associate verbal comprehension with intelligence and aptitude, so if an autistic person’s spiky profile has profound deficits in this area, they are often labeled as level three or requiring substantial support, and if their verbal comprehension is high, no matter how profound the other deficits, they are often told they “don’t seem autistic” or denied services they may need.

Recent findings suggest that I had a client a few years ago whose profile showed profound deficits in working memory and processing speed. He was unable to do basic living tasks like cleaning his room or brushing his teeth without support. Yet he was continuously told he didn’t need support and was denied support because his verbal comprehension was in the 99th percentile. Fluid reasoning is another part of IQ that people usually associate with high-functioning intelligence, and many autistic people are exceptional at spotting patterns, drawing inferences, or finding solutions to new problems and thus are assumed to be “high-functioning” or, in some cases, are told they “don’t seem” autistic.

This is the hardest part of being autistic. The spiky profile of skills and deficits is often profound in multiple areas, and people’s biases associated with aptitude and intelligence profoundly shape how much support and empathy an autistic person will get in their community at large. People think of the archetypal autistic person as being verbally awkward or less verbal, with stimming behaviors and no eye contact. But since this spiky profile is so variable in autistic people, they could have more profound deficits and be articulate and quiet and very able to mimic neurotypical social behaviors, but have a working memory that is so profoundly low that they can’t complete basic work-related or living tasks.

Recent findings suggest that I found my IQ test recently. My profile is typical for an autistic person. My verbal comprehension and fluid reasoning skills are in the 99.9th percentile, but my visual-spatial reasoning skills show profound deficits, and my working memory is also slightly impaired. This, combined with an inability to read most social cues, has made my life one of hostility from most neurotypicals. People perceive me as profoundly gifted. My IQ is high, and I am very articulate. People interpret this as pretentious and often accuse me of trying to “talk down to them”, but words are my natural habitat and my vocabulary is expansive. At the same time, I am an excellent problem solver, and I can easily find solutions to problems that confound others. Yet, mental rotations are almost impossible for me, and if I am asked to think in a room with more than one conversation or to multitask, I can shut down entirely. This, combined with the fact that I honestly misread most socially complex situations and offend people while trying to be nice or behave in ways I think are helpful but people find hurtful, makes people perceive me as a jerk instead of disabled.

This can go the other way. I have clients who are perceived as having an intellectual disability when, in many domains, they are gifted. They are never given the opportunity to show their strengths because people can’t see them.

My largest handicap is interpersonal interaction, and this is very evident in my personal life. This is largely due to my inability to see anything but the best in people and my spiky intellectual profile. After seeing me in several human interactions, my son was confounded and said, “You aren’t this stupid!” He listed all my accomplishments and said I couldn’t possibly be this dumb. He wasn’t being cruel. He was only coming to terms with the fact that the mother he had seen as brilliant and unbreakable had more disabilities than he thought were possible. This is a hard thing for a child to learn. Many people struggle with this discrepancy in me, and it erodes many of my relationships. Many people see my profound deficits as purposeful negligence.

In a world where autism acceptance and awareness are needed, I believe this is the part people need to understand the most about autistic people. Our “spiky profile” creates confusion in those around us. In the early 1990s, the film Rain Man created the archetypal image of a barely verbal autistic man with limited verbal skills who was inconceivably brilliant at math. I think it is crucial to remember that many autistic people are like this. We can seem like the smartest person in the room and at the same time be the most incapable person in the room.

Alvares, G. A., Bebbington, K., Cleary, D., Evans, K., Glasson, E. J., Maybery, M. T., Pillar, S., Uljarevic, M., Varcin, K., Wray, J., & Whitehouse, A. J. O. (2020). The misnomer of ‘high functioning autism’: Intelligence is an imprecise predictor of functional abilities in autism. Autism, 24(1), 221–232.

Dawson, M., Soulieres, I., Gernsbacher, M. A., & Mottron, L. (2007). The level and nature of autistic intelligence. Psychological Science, 18(8), 657–662.

#156724. Could a giant catapult launch someone to space? Short answer: Yes.

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1353 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Could a giant catapult launch someone to space? Short answer: Yes.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1353 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For as long as humans have looked at the night sky, we’ve wondered what lies beyond Earth—and dreamed up ways of getting up there.
  • Sources indicate that but what if, instead of modern rockets, we went medieval?
  • The answer requires a little imagination, a lot of physics, and a space-launching siege weapon of truly ridiculous proportions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For as long as humans have looked at the night sky, we’ve wondered what lies beyond Earth—and dreamed up ways of getting up there. These days, powerful rockets carrying tons of fuel are the tried-and-true method of escaping the planet’s gravitational pull and reaching space.

Sources indicate that but what if, instead of modern rockets, we went medieval? Could a trebuchet or catapult—the massive siege weapons once used to fling stones at castles—launch a person into orbit? And if so, just how major would one have to be?

The answer requires a little imagination, a lot of physics, and a space-launching siege weapon of truly ridiculous proportions.

Sources indicate that A catapult is essentially a giant lever used to hurl projectiles. Typically, they have a large, spoon-shaped throwing arm that’s wrenched back, creating tension, and then released, flinging an object over a great distance.

Sources indicate that A trebuchet is a kind of catapult that uses a counterweight and gravity to launch projectiles. This machine’s long arm rests on a fulcrum, with a sling or cup for the projectile at one end and a heavy counterweight at the other.

When the arm is released, gravity pulls the counterweight downward, sending the opposite end—and its payload—soaring upward and forward.

It has been revealed that trebuchets are typically more powerful than catapults because they can launch heavier payloads over greater distances. So for our purposes, we’ll be focusing on a space trebuchet rather than a space catapult.

Trebuchets have been hurling heavy objects through the air for centuries. The structures are believed to have originated in China as early as the fifth century BC and eventually spread across Eurasia, becoming a formidable force in medieval warfare.

They arrived in Europe during the 12th century and swiftly surpassed simple catapults.

It has been revealed that today, trebuchets are no longer used as weapons. But they remain popular as teaching tools for demonstrating physics principles—and for the decidedly more wholesome pursuit of seeing how far we can fling pumpkins, cabbages, and other projectiles.

So let’s crunch the numbers: Could a massive trebuchet really blast a human into orbit? Theoretically, yes. Practically, no.

For help answering this question, Popular Science turned to Frankie Zhu, an assistant professor in space robotics at the Colorado School of Mines in Golden, Colorado. Zhu gamely agreed to do some back-of-the-napkin math to put some numbers to this wildly improbable scenario.

“It just reminds me of a classic physics problem you would encounter in undergrad,” she states.

It has been revealed that before we can get to the heart of the calculations, Zhu claims, we need to define some initial parameters. First, because the energy required to send a human into orbit depends on both mass and velocity, we need to know our imaginary astronaut’s mass. Zhu recommends 70 kilograms, or about 154 pounds.

Next, we need to define where space—and, for our purposes, orbit—begins. The conventional boundary is the Kármán line, an imaginary line 100 kilometers (about 62 miles) above sea level that is widely used to mark the edge of space. It’s the point at which Earth’s atmosphere becomes too thin for conventional aircraft to generate enough lift to stay aloft. “An orbit at 100 kilometers would be the lowest energy orbit possible,” she indicates.

To orbit Earth at the Kármán line—and not plummet back to the ground—a person needs to travel at approximately 7.85 kilometers per second, or 17,500 miles per hour, the same speed the International Space Station travels while orbiting Earth. “Any less and the human would fly up and then come back down in a parabolic trajectory,” she indicates.

In a recent development, if we assume that the atmosphere doesn’t produce drag on the human as they fly, then the velocity of the person leaving the trebuchet immediately after launch needs to be at least 7.97 kilometers per second, or 17,828 miles per hour. That extra bit of speed accounts for the energy needed to climb from Earth’s surface to the Kármán line.

Sources indicate that to launch a human at that velocity, the trebuchet would need to store a massive amount of potential energy—about 2.22 billion joules, by Zhu’s calculations, similar to about 1,200 pounds of TNT. Zhu notes that she’s assuming 100 percent mechanical efficiency, meaning that none of the trebuchet’s stored energy is lost to friction, air resistance, sound, deformation, or the movement of the machine itself.

Industry observers note that from here, we can move on to the design of the trebuchet. Based on Zhu’s math, the trebuchet would need a 5,000-ton counterweight—the equivalent of roughly 950 African bush elephants—which would need to drop at least 45.2 meters, or roughly 148 feet.

To turn the relatively slow movement of the massive counterweight into a hypersonic launch speed, the trebuchet would need an extreme mechanical leverage ratio of 379:1, she says. With these figures in mind, the trebuchet’s long throwing arm—the part with the human at the end of it—would need to be about 17.14 kilometers, or 10.7 miles, long.

“That should give you all the physical parameters of the trebuchet, ignoring some physics and human welfare,” she jokes.

Industry observers note that how exactly would a human fare under these conditions? Fighter jet pilots can survive up to nine Gs using specialized G-suits, physical straining techniques, and intense centrifuge training. But, Zhu claims, the “amount of Gs that the trebuchet is going to reach is…definitely past nine Gs. This human is not going to be alive when they make it to orbit.”.

Sources indicate that another hurdle? Building the trebuchet. “To design a structure that can handle that amount of mass—the 5,000-ton counterweight—to support that mass and then to make something that large… that would be a humanity feat and a structural feat,” she notes.

How much trash is on the moon? About 412,000 pounds.

Why can’t we just launch all of Earth’s garbage into the sun?

What happens to your body when you die in space?

Is turbulence really like Jell-O? Pilots weigh in.

Recent findings suggest that why do we put seatbacks up for landing? An aviation expert explains.

A more human-friendly option, she says, might be a railgun, which uses electromagnetic forces to accelerate a projectile along a pair of conductive rails at extremely high speeds. To launch a person into orbit, a railgun would also need to be “really, really long,” she says. But because the human projectile could accelerate over a much greater distance and for a longer period of time, a railgun would theoretically offer a smoother acceleration profile—one that’s more amenable to human survival.

“Whereas [with] a trebuchet, the acceleration is going to be impulsive,” she claims. “It’s going to be a huge smack at the very beginning if the structure doesn’t flex, if the structure is rigid.”.

It has been revealed that rockets have been the standard for launching things into space since 1944, when Germany’s V-2 became the first human-made object to cross the Kármán line. But that doesn’t necessarily mean they’re the most efficient way to get there.

Rockets require enormous amounts of fuel, and all of that propellant has to be carried onboard. In other words, a rocket has to spend fuel lifting not just its payload, but also the fuel it needs to keep accelerating. This makes getting off Earth an inherently energy-intensive—and expensive—proposition.

Sources indicate that with that in mind, engineers continue to explore other ways of getting into space, ideally using less fuel and resources. So far, though, most of their ideas haven’t made it off the drawing board—and, after crunching the numbers, Zhu says it’s highly unlikely that trebuchets will ever replace rockets.

“A lot of ideas are fantastical, some are possible, and an even smaller set are economical,” notes Zhu.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Somehow, after all these years, there are still a considerable number of vehicles equipped with Takata airbags, though their number should be considerably lower in the near future. Honda just issued a recall for 810,592 cars equipped with Takata airbags that could rupture due to propellant degradation caused by high humidity.

Industry observers note that according to documents filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), the recall covers some 2013 Acura RDX, ILX, Honda CR-V, Civic, and Accord models. The affected Accords and Acuras are all from the 2013 model year, while the CR-V and Civic populations include both 2012 and 2013 vehicles.

See all results for used cars for sale near 29405.

In a recent development, the NHTSA documents show that the affected vehicles are equipped with airbag inflators that use a phase-stabilized ammonium nitrate propellant, which is intended to control moisture within the inflator. Over time, exposure to high humidity and repeated temperature changes can cause the inflator to become brittle. When the brittle inflators are deployed, they could turn into projectiles that shoot metal fragments through the cabin, potentially injuring or killing occupants.

According to recent reports, the recall comes after years of investigation and analysis by Honda, which was routinely shared with NHTSA. The recall documents show that on November 19, 2026, Honda determined that the inflators posed enough of a risk to warrant the new recall.

Sources indicate that owners of affected models will be contacted by mail and urged to bring their vehicle to a Honda or Acura dealership. Dealer technicians will replace the driver and passenger airbag inflators with a different model for free. Dealers have already been notified of the recall, with owner notification letters scheduled to be sent on December 18. Owners concerned that their car might be included in the recall can check on the NHTSA recalls site as well as NHTSA’s dedicated Takata airbag recall page.
