#156722. Breaking: BYD in talks to buy Ineos’ French factory as Grenadier moves to US

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1249 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: BYD in talks to buy Ineos’ French factory as Grenadier moves to US

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1249 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The French factory Mercedes built for the tiny Smart city car, and that Jim Ratcliffe turned into the home of his Land Rover Defender tribute, could soon be building BYDs.
  • Sources indicate that BYD confirmed today that it has entered exclusive negotiations to acquire Ineos Automotive’s plant in Hambach, France.
  • According to recent reports, the other half of the deal is Ineos packing up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The French factory Mercedes built for the tiny Smart city car, and that Jim Ratcliffe turned into the home of his Land Rover Defender tribute, could soon be building BYDs.

Sources indicate that BYD confirmed today that it has entered exclusive negotiations to acquire Ineos Automotive’s plant in Hambach, France. If it closes, it would be the Chinese giant’s second passenger car factory in the EU after Hungary, and the first time a Chinese automaker buys an existing car plant in Europe.

According to recent reports, the other half of the deal is Ineos packing up. Alongside the announcement, Ineos Automotive noted it looks to move Grenadier and Quartermaster production to the US, which it says accounts for about 70% of its sales. It has shortlisted US sites, hasn’t named any, and is aiming to start production there in 2028.

Recent findings suggest that the math is simple. Every Grenadier shipped from France to the US gets hit with a 15% tariff, and the Quartermaster pickup falls under the 25% tariff on imported pickups. When 7 out of 10 of your customers are American, building your trucks in Lorraine stops making sense.

Ineos indicates it will keep building both models at Hambach “for the medium term” if the sale goes through, so the two companies would share the site for a while.

Recent findings suggest that neither side disclosed a price or a closing date, and the sale still has to go through consultation with employee representatives. BYD will soon find out that France is nothing like China when it comes to employee representation. There’s also no word yet on which BYD models would come out of Hambach or when. Same for the plant’s roughly 1,000 employees: BYD made no commitment on how many it would keep.

BYD executive vice president Stella Li said the organization wants to give European consumers “vehicles built in France” that use BYD’s technology.

Hambach opened in 1997 as “Smartville,” Mercedes’ factory for the Smart Fortwo, and it later built the all-electric Smart EQ Fortwo. Ineos bought it from Mercedes at the end of 2020 after dropping its initiative to build a new factory in Wales, and Grenadier production started in 2022. Ineos notes it has put nearly €540 million into the site since 2019.

Sources indicate that capacity is about 30,000 Grenadiers a year. That’s not much by BYD’s standards. BYD sold 3,561,615 passenger vehicles globally in the first 10 months of the year, which means 30,000 units is less than three days of its output.

There’s also a bit of irony in who’s buying. Ineos unveiled its first EV, the Fusilier, in early 2024 while romanticizing gas cars at the same event. A few months later, it shelved the electric model indefinitely, blaming “reluctant consumer uptake” of EVs. Now it’s selling its only factory to the world’s largest EV maker.

Industry observers note that this isn’t a surprise. Back in May, Stella Li noted BYD was in talks with Stellantis and “other companies too” to take over underused plants in Europe, and that BYD would rather own and run a plant than form a joint venture. Hambach fits that description exactly.

Recent findings suggest that BYD’s first European car plant, in Szeged, Hungary, started trial production earlier this year and is expected to reach mass production in early 2027, with the Dolphin Surf and Atto 2 first in line. BYD eventually wants more than 150,000 vehicles a year out of it. Its separate factory project in Turkey has been put on pause.

The motivation is regulatory. China-built BYD EVs face a 17% countervailing duty in the EU on top of the standard 10% car tariff, imported Chinese hybrids are now subject to quotas, and the EU’s proposed “Made in Europe” rules would tie EV subsidies and public contracts to how much of a vehicle is built locally. A French plant solves a lot of those problems at once.

And BYD isn’t alone. Leapmotor started building the B10 at Stellantis’ Zaragoza plant in Spain in October, Dongfeng prepares to build cars at a Stellantis factory in France, Geely is reportedly lining up a Ford plant in Spain, and Chery already assembles vehicles in Barcelona.

Sources indicate that chery is the one BYD should watch. Through October, BYD registered 320,445 vehicles in Europe, up 133%, according to Automotive News. Chery Group was just ahead with 320,631, up 235%. A gap of 186 cars.

Europe matters more than ever for BYD because home isn’t going well. BYD brand sales in China fell 40% to 1,544,699 vehicles over the first 10 months, and its global passenger vehicle sales are down 2.7%.

Recent findings suggest that this is a smart, cheap move for BYD. Building Szeged took years, including land disputes with private owners. Hambach comes with a trained workforce, a paint shop, a supplier base on the German border, and a seller that’s motivated to leave. You don’t get a much easier entry into France, but the easiest in France is still probably more difficult than anything BYD faced in China when it comes to deploying latest production capacity.

Industry observers note that the 30,000-unit capacity is small, but BYD isn’t buying it for what it builds today. It’s buying a “Made in France” label ahead of local content rules.

Recent findings suggest that I'm guessing BYD is gambling on the French not making it too difficult as it would deter future investment. They're probably also going to use a lot of robots.

Recent findings suggest that we also can’t ignore the symmetry here. Ineos is leaving Europe to build in the US because of tariffs. BYD is buying into Europe because of tariffs. That’s protectionism moving factories. Europe keeps the jobs, and the workers who used to build Smart EVs might get to build EVs again.

And yes, it’s funny that BYD is moving into the home of the Grenadier, a vehicle that exists because Ratcliffe loved the old Defender, days after a court in The Hague barred BYD’s Ti7 from the EU for infringing Land Rover’s Defender design.

The real question is what BYD puts on the line in Hambach. If it’s battery-electric cars, great. If it’s plug-in hybrids built to get around quotas, Europe is trading one gas-burning 4×4 factory for another.

Industry News: Fresh Zealand’s Twin-Engine Toyota Celica Is Essentially Unstoppable

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the art of modifying cars is gleefully rule-free.
  • It has been revealed that wadsworth’s twin-engine Toyota Celica has made literal waves on social video in the past few weeks, as the Christchurch resident demonstrated its remarkable wading abilities in a series of viral videos.
  • It has been revealed that with so many moving parts, Wadsworth went analog with the controls; a pulley system attached to the original clutch pedal also operates the clutch for the rear transmission, and the throttle pedal is divided into an upper portion for the front engine and a lower portion for the rear engine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the art of modifying cars is gleefully rule-free. Sure, there are never-ending hoops to jump through for street legality, but actually building your perfect vehicle is merely a matter of dreams. For Kiwi Gareth Wadsworth, who goes by @garethcars on social media, those dreams meant stuffing two engines and two transmissions into a single sixth-generation Toyota Celica. Seems easy enough, right?

It has been revealed that wadsworth’s twin-engine Toyota Celica has made literal waves on social video in the past few weeks, as the Christchurch resident demonstrated its remarkable wading abilities in a series of viral videos. The basic recipe is a pair of Toyota’s 2.0-liter 3S-GE engines—one mounted in the front and one mounted in the rear—mated to a pair of manual transmissions and fed to individual differentials.

It has been revealed that with so many moving parts, Wadsworth went analog with the controls; a pulley system attached to the original clutch pedal also operates the clutch for the rear transmission, and the throttle pedal is divided into an upper portion for the front engine and a lower portion for the rear engine. If you press directly in the middle of the accelerator, both engines will rev up (somewhat) in sync. Wadsworth emphasized that it is two completely separate drivetrains that require two of everything (two batteries, two fuel tanks, two ECUs, two radiators) and can be driven separately or simultaneously.

Recent findings suggest that but this Celica build wasn’t always this extreme. In fact, the initial version was supposed to be a simple overlanding setup for a university off-road club trip in 2020. He initially off-roaded the Celica with a simple four-inch lift kit and 31-inch tires, but Wadsworth wanted to try something more extreme—and he didn’t want to abandon the existing platform.

It has been revealed that “I had this Celica that I bought crashed, and I didn't have anything to do with it. I was a student. I didn't have the money for a four-wheel-drive, so I ended up building it into a four-wheel-drive,” Wadsworth said to Road & Track. “I paid $800 for the car, and then I sold the wheels and tires that were on it. So it was effectively a free car just sitting around, and I got some suspension left over from other projects that I threw in it, and the engine came from a crashed car I found upside down off the side of the road.”.

According to recent reports, after a year of mud-slinging fun, Wadsworth decided to go all-in on the dual-engine swap. The rear engine transplant only took two weeks, with most of the work happening after school and during a series of all-nighters. A day or two after the build was complete, Wadsworth and friends trailered the dual-engine Celica to an off-road area and began testing its abilities. Some limitations were quickly revealed.

Sources indicate that “It was just the stock intakes for a few trips. It did have a snorkel on the outside for the front engine. Once it was twin-engine, it had enough power that we could hit the water faster, and that meant that the bow wave would keep going over the roof and filling the front engine's snorkel. We had one trip on the White Bear River that was in flood, and we hydrolocked the front engine twenty-three times, and we got sick of having to pull the spark plugs out, blasting the water out, and trying to get it running again. And so that's why I moved the intake to the glove box,” Wadsworth said.

Wading is one of the twin-engine Celica’s best tricks, as it is fast enough to glide onto the water and light enough to float through. The Celica has floated through currents that have sunk heavier 4x4 trucks, Wadsworth remarked. But the twin-engine Celica doesn’t just excel at water crossings, either. Because the gearboxes run independently, Wadsworth can tune the gear ratios of either end to suit his needs.

Sources indicate that “There's no weird handling from the differences between the front and rear. It's just whichever engine's got the least load on it speeds up to catch up with the other one. They're effectively a fifty-fifty split,” Wadsworth noted. “Because of the biasing, I quite often run almost exclusively rear-wheel-drive, and I only add front when I need it for traction. It's quite a unique feeling. It's so much fun, and probably the main reason I've still got it is being able to dynamically shift between front, rear, or four-wheel-drive and throttle biasing on the fly. In a mud pit, I can sit around doing donuts with the front in neutral, and then I can put the front-end gear in and let the clutch out slowly on the front to transition from donuts to power slides.”.

In a recent development, and it isn’t even too hard to drive—relatively speaking. Wadsworth mentioned that his mates can hop in and romp it with minimal coaching, at least in this configuration. Shifting the two gearboxes can get awkward, but the rear transmission shifter is placed near the traditional shifter, so you don’t have to reach far. Before the pulley clutch system, Wadsworth wired the rear clutch through the parking brake, which required a gentle touch to keep from stalling.

Recent findings suggest that but it wasn’t always so accommodating. “On the original build, we didn't have time to connect any of the controls, so it had two drivers back then. And we didn't have a throttle, so the strap for tightening the hood was tied onto the rearview mirror and back to the rear throttle body, and you pulled it like a train horn,” Wadsworth stated. “We certainly had a lot of difficulty driving it when we first built it, because it required two people to communicate—but it didn't have any exhaust, so we couldn't hear each other, and we had no total control on the rear; it was either fully on or fully off. And you had to get up out of your seat, turn around, and put it in gear for the rear engine.”.

Recent findings suggest that even after six years of ownership and five years with two engines, Wadsworth intends to continue driving the twin-engine Celica as long as possible. Initially, he considered adding four-wheel steering using a power steering motor from a Nissan Leaf, but he stated the time under the knife wouldn’t be worth it. The more time spent off-road, the better.

The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (806 w)

Does Menopausal Hormone Therapy Lower Dementia Risk? Timing and Genetics May Hold the Answer

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women who have longer reproductive life spans or use menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) may have better brain health as they age, according to a new study.
  • The research, published November 4 in Neurology, found that longer lifetime exposure to estrogen was associated with fewer signs of damage to small blood vessels in the brain.
  • The findings could offer newly introduced insights into the relationship between estrogen and brain aging, particularly as women account for approximately two-thirds of Alzheimer’s disease cases worldwide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women who have longer reproductive life spans or use menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) may have better brain health as they age, according to a new study.

The research, published November 4 in Neurology, found that longer lifetime exposure to estrogen was associated with fewer signs of damage to small blood vessels in the brain.

The findings could offer newly introduced insights into the relationship between estrogen and brain aging, particularly as women account for approximately two-thirds of Alzheimer’s disease cases worldwide.

Researchers also found that certain associations between hormone therapy and brain health differed depending on whether women carried a genetic variant associated with an increased risk of Alzheimer’s disease.

In a recent development, however, the relationship between estrogen and brain health is complex. While the findings suggest that longer estrogen exposure may be associated with healthier brain aging, they do not establish that hormone therapy can prevent Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.

The researchers drew data from the Gothenburg H70-1944 Birth Cohort, a longitudinal study of 1,203 individuals born in 1944 who resided in Gothenburg, Sweden.

The final cohort included 352 cisgender women, with an average age of 70, who had no neurological disorders and reliable self-reported data on their estrogen exposure.

According to recent reports, individual estrogen exposure was measured through structured interviews. It included:.

The researchers used this information as a proxy for lifetime estrogen exposure, though the study didn’t measure actual hormone levels.

Participants were also given a brain MRI at baseline and then again at a 5-year follow-up.

In a recent development, the researchers found that those with a longer reproductive span had a lower risk of small vessel disease (SVD). Participants with a longer reproductive life span had an 8% lower risk of having two or more signs of SVD. However, later menopause, rather than earlier menstruation, appeared to be the main driver of this association.

Those who used MHT also tended to have fewer signs of SVD and better microstructural integrity in the white matter.

Industry observers note that in individuals who carried the APOE-ε4 variant, which increases a person’s risk of Alzheimer’s disease, MHT was associated with greater cortical thickness in brain regions vulnerable to Alzheimer’s disease. However, there was no association for those without this variant.

The researchers noted that longer estrogen exposure was associated with stable cortical thickness and white matter trajectories over time.

Dung Trinh, MD, internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and Chief Medical Officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that estrogen has several vital effects on the brain that may help support cognitive health.

It influences communication between brain cells, supports the brain’s ability to use glucose for energy, helps regulate neurotransmitters, and plays a role in maintaining healthy blood vessels and reducing inflammation and oxidative stress.

“As estrogen levels decline during menopause, some of these protective effects may diminish. Replacing estrogen closer to the menopause transition could potentially help preserve some of these functions during a vulnerable period for brain health,” he said. “While these findings are encouraging, MHT has not been proven to prevent Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.”.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who also wasn’t involved in the study, agreed and noted, “Starting menopausal hormone therapy earlier in the menopause transition may help minimize some changes by supporting the brain during this period of hormonal fluctuation.”.

“There is growing interest in whether early estrogen therapy may also help reduce the long-term risk of Alzheimer’s disease, although more research is needed before we can establish that benefit,” she added.

Ross told Healthline that this research reinforces the importance of recognizing menopause as more than a reproductive or hormonal transition.

According to recent reports, “We know that women are disproportionately affected by dementia and Alzheimer’s disease, and some women experience noticeable cognitive changes beginning in perimenopause,” she said. “If future research confirms that starting hormone therapy earlier can help protect long-term cognitive health, it could influence how we approach menopause treatment and encourage more proactive conversations between women and their healthcare providers.”.

“The goal should be to individualize treatment based on a woman’s symptoms, medical history, and overall health rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach,” Ross added.

Trinh agreed that an individualized approach to menopause management is important.

“This does not mean that every woman should start hormone therapy to prevent dementia. Instead, it highlights the importance of understanding which women might benefit, when treatment should begin, and which formulations are most appropriate,” he mentioned. “Factors such as age, time since menopause, cardiovascular risk, metabolic health, family history, and potentially genetic factors may all help guide future recommendations.”.

“We still need stronger clinical evidence before changing current prescribing guidelines specifically for dementia prevention,” Trinh added.

Smart home gift guide: 40 clever gadgets to make any living space better using automation

The best smart home gift is the one that works the day it’s unwrapped, without a ladder, a landlord’s sign-off, or a surprise subscription. This guide covers every type of smart home dweller, from beginner to full-on Tony Stark. We started with easy plug-and-play options like a four-pack of Kasa Matter smart plugs and Philips Hue Essential bulbs that get up and running in minutes, along with fresh 2026 hardware we’ve tested hands-on, like Apple’s HomeView display. At the other end, upgrades like the Nest Learning Thermostat and the Emporia Vue 3 energy monitor reward a little more installation work.

Sources indicate that before you buy, find out which smart home platform your recipient already uses. Alexa, Google Home, and Apple Home still don’t share everything, though Matter-certified gear like the Eve Energy plug and the Govee Floor Lamp 2 works with all three. Some Matter devices connect over Thread, a low-power wireless network that needs a hub called a border router, such as a HomePod mini 2 or a Google TV Streamer, to reach the rest of the house. The entries flag the hubs, extra hardware, and monthly plans that can turn a gift into homework. Prices come from makers and major retailers and were checked in November 2026, so expect them to move during holiday sales.

If you’re shopping for a cook, the smart ovens and smokers are in our kitchen gift guide. If you’re building out a whole system rather than shopping for one gift, start with our guide to the best smart home devices.

The Dot gets a built-in smart home hub.

In a recent development, amazon kept the old shape and changed the guts inside. The sixth-generation Echo Dot adds a built-in smart home hub for Zigbee, Matter, and Thread gear, so it can pair devices on its own instead of leaning on a separate bridge. Amazon also claims 50 percent more bass than the model it replaces, though anyone buying primarily for music should watch for holiday discounts or spend $20 more on the Echo Dot Max. Its built-in eero extender stretches Wi-Fi by up to 1,000 square feet in houses that already run eero, and Alexa+ is included with Prime or costs $19.99 a month without it.

An all-in-one gift for backyard birdwatchers, the Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro pairs 4K HDR with PDAF Auto Focus for sharp close-ups, plus 1080p/120 fps slow motion for fleeting moments. FeatherPal AI identifies more than 10,000 species with an eligible subscription, while the 5W solar roof and removable hopper simplify upkeep. Now $199.99—save $60 at its lowest price of the year through December 27.

Google’s first newly introduced speaker in six years.

Google went six years without a newly introduced smart speaker before the Google Home Speaker arrived in June. Built around Gemini for Home, it includes a Thread border router and handles everyday jobs like switching lights and adjusting a thermostat without a subscription. Gemini Live conversations and extra AI features require Google Home Premium, which starts at $10 a month. Buy it for someone who already runs their house from the Google Home app.

The hub that makes Apple Home work away from home.

For a household built around iPhones, the HomePod mini 2 is the speaker that lets Apple’s Home app run automations and control gear from away. It runs on an S10 chip with Wi-Fi 6E and Thread, acting as a hub for HomeKit and Matter accessories. Buy it for that hub job first: Apple states Siri’s bigger AI upgrades arrive in a future software update, and the personal features need an iPhone or iPad that supports Apple Intelligence. An Apple TV 4K handles the same hub duties for anyone who would rather have a streaming box.

Apple’s first smart display doubles as a home hub.

Apple’s first smart display, HomeView, puts a 7-inch touchscreen on the kitchen counter for music, FaceTime calls, and Apple Home controls, while serving as a home hub alongside the HomePod mini 2. In our hands-on review, we found it very helpful, if a little quirky.

Recent findings suggest that it recognizes up to six people by face and surfaces their own messages, calendars, and reminders, though only when that person’s paired iPhone or iPad is nearby and recently unlocked. Stick to the tabletop model as a gift: the wall-mounted version starts at the same $299, but it requires a separate Schneider Home wall mount starting at $59.95 (plus a user-supplied 20-watt USB-C power adapter for the base mount).

Hue color bulbs without the bridge.

Philips Hue used to be the smart bulb you bought only after getting serious about smart home tech. The Hue Essential line changes the math with an affordable four-pack of color bulbs that connect over Bluetooth and work from the Hue app without a bridge. Each bulb puts out 800 lumens and dims down to 2 percent. Adding them to Alexa, Google Home, or Apple Home runs through Matter and takes a compatible hub, such as an Echo, a Nest Hub, or a HomePod mini 2, and they can always move onto a Hue Bridge later.

Two color bulbs that work with every major platform.

In a recent development, A pair of GE Cync Full Color bulbs is a low-stakes way to test smart lighting on two bedside lamps. They connect straight to 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi in the Cync app with no hub, and Matter support brings them into Alexa, Google Home, Apple Home, and SmartThings when paired with a compatible Matter hub. Each puts out 800 lumens, matching the Hue Essential bulbs above, and if the recipient hates smart home gear, they still work like regular bulbs.

Four plugs that work with every major assistant.

Recent findings suggest that this four-pack of Kasa Matter smart plugs is the easiest way to automate something your recipient already owns, whether that’s a lamp, a holiday tree, or a coffee maker. Each slim plug leaves the second wall outlet free, handles up to 15 amps, tracks energy use, and connects to Apple Home, Alexa, and Google Home through Matter. Just note that they only join a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi network.

Local control, no account required.

Buy Eve Energy for someone who doesn’t want a living-room lamp checking in with a company server. Eve indicates it needs no cloud account or registration, and it communicates locally over Matter and Thread while tracking power draw. Because it relies on Thread, the house needs a border router like a HomePod mini 2 or a Google TV Streamer. At $39.95, you’re paying nearly as much for one plug as you would for the Kasa four-pack above.

Two outlets for the lights on the porch.

Recent findings suggest that the GE Cync Outdoor Smart Plug puts holiday lights and porch string lights on two independently controlled outlets rated for wet locations, with covers for both sockets and a 15-amp ceiling. This model connects to Alexa and Google Assistant straight over Wi-Fi. Its Amazon listing doesn’t mention Apple Home, so iPhone households should look for GE’s newer Matter-compatible version instead.

Four outlets that work with Apple Home too.

Competition for outlets is fierce behind my desk and TV. It’s probably like that for you, too. The Meross Smart Power Strip has four outlets that switch independently, so the TV, the game console and the lamp behind them can each follow a different schedule. Its four USB ports switch as a group, and surge protection is built in. It connects over 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi with no hub and works with Apple Home, Alexa, Google Home and SmartThings, though controlling it through Apple Home from outside the house takes a home hub like a HomePod mini 2.

Color accent lighting for Apple, Google and Alexa homes.

Despite what an electrician will tell you, it’s possible to revamp a room’s lighting without breaking into the wiring. The Govee Floor Lamp 2 is rated for up to 1,725 lumens, with independent lighting for the pole and base. Matter support drops it straight into Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa, or SmartThings without a Govee-only workaround, though it ships in pieces, so strategy on a few minutes of assembly.

Christmas lights that know the shape of the tree.

Industry observers note that unlike standard app-controlled holiday lights that just change color, Twinkly Strings use a phone’s camera to map where every bulb sits on the tree, then animate patterns across that exact shape. This 100-LED Gen II strand connects over Wi-Fi and Bluetooth and can’t be cut to length. Twinkly indicates you can sync up to 4,000 LEDs across multiple sets, which helps, since 100 bulbs won’t cover a full-size tree on their own.

Give the Hatch Restore 3 to anyone who dreads a phone alarm blaring six inches from their face. It brightens gradually like a sunrise in the morning and handles wind-down lighting and sound at night. Sunrise alarms, wind-down lights, and a basic sound library all work without a subscription, while the optional Hatch+ sleep library runs $5.99 a month or $59.99 a year after a 30-day free trial.

Family photos with no subscription.

Family members add photos and videos to the Aura Carver from Aura’s app, so upcoming pictures keep showing up long after the holidays, with no subscription and no storage limit. The 10.1-inch landscape screen pairs two portrait shots side by side so they fill the display. You can preload photos before it ships so it comes out of the box ready to go. Just double-check which album you pick before Grandma gets an unexpected slideshow.

Sized for a bedroom, controlled from a phone.

In a recent development, this gift doesn’t have to be passive-aggressive, but it can be. Levoit recommends the Core 300S-P for bedrooms and offices up to 219 square feet, since the 1,058-square-foot figure in its listings assumes only one air change an hour. It connects to the free VeSync app for remote control, responds to Alexa and Google Assistant, and ships with a three-stage filter already installed alongside an indicator that flags when it needs replacing.

Answers the question of whether the cat ate.

Industry observers note that the Petlibro Granary Smart Camera Feeder answers the question every pet owner texts the sitter: Did the cat eat? It holds 5 liters of kibble, connects over 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz Wi-Fi, and schedules dry-food meals from an app while watching the bowl with a 1080p, 145-degree night-vision camera and two-way audio. Petlibro’s Video Cloud plans start at $59.99 a year for seven days of storage, or clips can be saved locally to a microSD card (sold separately).

A TV box with a smart home hub inside.

According to recent reports, think of the Google TV Streamer as an entertaining Trojan horse for sneaking a smart hub into the living room. Beyond 4K HDR with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos, it doubles as a Matter hub and Thread border router, anchoring gear like the Eve Energy plug and putting a home control panel right on the TV. Google doesn’t include an HDMI cable, so tuck one into the gift bag.

Person and pet alerts without a monthly bill.

Recent findings suggest that unwrapping a gadget that immediately hands you a monthly bill is a terrible gift experience, which is why the Tapo C120 keeps its subscription optional. It distinguishes people, pets, and vehicles without a paid plan and saves footage to a microSD card up to 512 GB (not included). You get 2K QHD video, color night vision from dual spotlights, Alexa and Google Assistant support, and an IP66 rating for outdoor use wherever an outlet is in reach of its power cord. Tapo Care cloud storage is there only if you want it.

2K video on a rechargeable battery.

For a front door without existing wiring, the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K (2nd gen) runs on a built-in rechargeable battery and records Retinal 2K video with 6× zoom. Ring’s $49.99 Solar Charger keeps it topped up for anyone who doesn’t want to pull it off the frame to recharge. Saving and reviewing clips does require a Ring subscription, with Ring Solo covering one device for $4.99 a month.

A smart lock that keeps the landlord’s key working.

Because the SwitchBot Lock Ultra mounts over the inside thumbturn of an existing deadbolt, renters get smart access without replacing the cylinder or cutting off the landlord’s key.

In a recent development, this Vision Combo bundles a keypad that unlocks with 3D facial recognition alongside a Hub Mini for remote control and Apple Home, Alexa, and Google Home support. Some deadbolt shapes need a separate $20 adapter kit, so take a quick look at the door before you wrap it.

A tiny robot finger for the coffee maker.

According to recent reports, sticking a SwitchBot Bot next to a coffee maker or air conditioner gives an old appliance a tiny robotic finger to push its button on command. It sticks next to a rocker switch or push button with an adhesive pad. Out of the box, it runs over Bluetooth in the SwitchBot app; remote access and voice commands through Alexa, Google Assistant, or Siri require a separate SwitchBot hub.

The battery-powered Hue Dimmer Switch puts a real button back on the wall for houseguests, mounting with adhesive or screws and lifting off its magnetic plate to work from the couch. It dims Hue lights and cycles through scenes, and Hue’s setup guide says it can pair directly with up to 10 bulbs. App customization and routines still require a Hue Bridge, so it makes the most sense for someone who already owns one.

Turns an opening door into a trigger.

Recent findings suggest that stick the Aqara Door and Window Sensor P2 on a door or window, and opening it can switch on a hall light or fire off a phone alert. It runs on a CR123A battery and joins Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa, or SmartThings over Matter and Thread. Make sure the recipient already has a Thread border router like the HomePod mini 2 or Google TV Streamer, because the sensor won’t work without one.

Three sensors for the spots that flood first.

A leak sensor may seem like a boring gift until you consider the pain of a water heater disaster. This GoveeLife Water Leak Detector 1s kit bundles three IP67-rated sensors and a Wi-Fi gateway that sends a phone alert when one of them gets wet, while each puck sounds a 105-decibel alarm. Govee claims five years of battery life. Tuck them under the water heater, the washing machine, and the kitchen sink.

Sprinkler smarts for a garden hose.

The Rachio Smart Hose Timer threads onto an outdoor faucet, runs schedules from Rachio’s app, and skips a watering when rain is in the forecast. The starter kit includes one valve and the 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi hub it requires, and a single hub can manage up to eight valves. Grab a pair of AA batteries (not included), and in cold climates remind the recipient it’s a gift for spring that needs to come indoors before a hard freeze.

Solar power, two lenses and no monthly bill.

Industry observers note that mounted outdoor cameras are a pain to pull down for charging, so the eufy SoloCam S340 brings its own solar panel, which eufy notes stays topped up on two hours of direct sun a day. It pairs a 3K wide-angle lens and a 2K telephoto lens for 8× hybrid zoom, pans 344 degrees, saves clips to 8 GB of built-in storage with no monthly fee, and works with Alexa and Google Assistant. At full MSRP, it sits just $10 under eufy’s newer SoloCam E50 ($229.99), so watch for holiday discounts on the S340 or check which model the listing reveals.

The alarm Google sells now that the Nest Protect is gone.

Google stopped making the Nest Protect, and the First Alert SC5 is the smart alarm the Google Store sells in its place. It detects smoke and carbon monoxide, sends phone alerts, and can be checked, silenced, or tested from the First Alert or Google Home apps. It even interconnects with existing Nest Protects so every unit sounds together, making it a timely drop-in swap as older Nest Protects reach their expiration dates after about 10 years. This battery model needs no wiring, though homes with hardwired alarms should opt for First Alert’s hardwired version instead.

Comes with a sensor for the room that’s always too hot.

Recent findings suggest that our utility bills went haywire last year, and that makes the math on a smart thermostat much more attractive. Google’s fourth-generation Nest Learning Thermostat includes a Nest Temperature Sensor for the room that never feels right, is designed to work in most homes without a common power wire (C-wire), and supports Matter so it also reveals up in Apple Home. It’s sold only in the U.S. and Canada.

A thermostat that also watches the air.

Industry observers note that the ecobee Smart Thermostat Premium packs a lot onto one wall plate: radar occupancy detection, an indoor air quality monitor, and a built-in Alexa speaker, plus a remote SmartSensor in the box. Siri works on it too in homes that already have a HomePod or HomePod mini 2. The company claims it can cut heating and cooling costs by up to 26 percent, or as much as $284 a year, and fit more than 95 percent of HVAC systems.

Unlocks with a tap of an iPhone or Apple Watch.

The Schlage Encode Plus is the deadbolt to buy for iPhone households, unlocking with a tap of an iPhone or Apple Watch via Apple Home Keys while also supporting Alexa and Google Assistant. Built-in Wi-Fi means no separate bridge for the Schlage app, Alexa, or Google, though remote Apple Home control takes a home hub like a HomePod mini 2 or Apple TV.

Schlage’s app manages up to 100 access codes for guests and dog walkers, and a physical backup key comes in the box. Schlage estimates four AA batteries last up to six months with typical use. Because it replaces the whole deadbolt, confirm the recipient is allowed to swap theirs before wrapping it.

Smart lights that survive someone flipping the switch.

Put the Lutron Diva smart dimmer on your list for anyone tired of guests killing smart bulbs at the wall. It replaces the switch with a familiar paddle, and this starter kit bundles Lutron’s Caséta hub and a Pico remote to tie the lights into Alexa, Apple Home, Google Home, Ring, and Sonos. Better yet, it handles up to 150 watts of LEDs without needing a neutral wire (the extra return wire missing from many older switch boxes).

No more driving back to check the garage.

According to recent reports, the Meross MSG100HK puts an end to circling back down the street to check whether the garage door closed. It wires into an existing opener instead of replacing the motor, requires no subscription, and covers Apple Home, Alexa, and Google Assistant. Run the opener through Meross’s compatibility checker first, since Chamberlain, LiftMaster, and Craftsman units may need a separate accessory that Meross ships at no charge.

Skips the watering when it already rained.

It has been revealed that rachio has sold the Rachio 3 for years, and it’s still the manufacturer’s main sprinkler controller. It replaces the timer on an existing in-ground irrigation system, installs in 30 minutes or less according to Rachio, and runs on a free app with weather skips that hold off on watering after rain. A 16-zone version costs $249.99, and the controller pairs with the Tempest weather station further down this list.

Find out which circuit is eating the electric bill.

The Emporia Vue 3 shows which circuits are eating the electric bill, though it can’t separate two appliances that share a circuit. The kit includes two main sensors and 16 branch sensors, and the company claims customers save an average of 10 percent on their bills.

Those sensors clamp onto wires inside the breaker panel, so initiative on an electrician unless the recipient is qualified to work in one.

Radon, particulates and CO2 in one box.

For anyone who wonders what’s floating around their house, with or without a basement, the Airthings View Plus tracks odorless radon alongside fine dust (PM2.5), carbon dioxide, chemical fumes (VOCs), humidity, temperature, and air pressure with no subscription. Airthings states it runs up to two years on six AA batteries, or it can stay plugged in over USB-C.

Self-emptying, and no bags to buy.

According to recent reports, the Eureka E20 Evo Plus docks at a bagless self-emptying station, so there are no replacement bags to reorder. It’s rated for 10,000 Pa of suction and maps rooms with lidar. Eureka notes the station’s 2-liter bin needs emptying every couple of weeks in a typical home, though the trade-off is dumping that dusty bin into the trash by hand.

A backyard weather station with no moving parts.

Turn a backyard into a personal weather lab with the Tempest Weather Station. It uses zero moving parts, measuring wind with ultrasonic sensors and rain with a haptic sensor, and feeds those readings into its own local forecasts with no subscription. The 2026 revision adds bigger solar panels and a replaceable battery.

It integrates with Alexa, Siri, IFTTT, and Rachio, so a rainy morning can cancel the sprinklers automatically. A flat base and pole mount come in the box, but supplying the actual fence post or mast in an open spot is up to the buyer.

Turns existing Hue bulbs into motion sensors.

In a recent development, anyone with a pile of Hue bulbs will get more out of a Hue Bridge Pro than another lamp. It supports more than 150 lights, and Philips notes it responds five times faster than the standard bridge. Its MotionAware feature turns groups of three or four compatible Hue bulbs into motion sensors that switch lights on automatically, though security motion alerts and alarms require a paid strategy.

One interface for a house full of gadgets.

Sources indicate that for the person who already owns half of this list, the next gift is a single interface to wrangle it all. Home Assistant Green arrives with the open-source Home Assistant software preinstalled, plugs into a router over Ethernet, and packs 4 GB of RAM and 32 GB of storage. Zigbee gear requires a separate Home Assistant Connect ZBT-2 adapter.

According to recent reports, the software is free and runs locally inside the house. Reaching it remotely, or linking it to Alexa or Google Assistant, takes either networking know-how or Nabu Casa’s optional Home Assistant Link subscription ($6.50 a month or $65 a year). Nabu Casa raised the box’s suggested price to $199 this year, citing memory costs.

#156717. Tech Report: Can Pirelli’s Cyber Tyre Technology Replace Drive Modes?

Tech Report: Can Pirelli’s Cyber Tyre Technology Replace Drive Modes?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (959 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Caranddriver

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After roughly 25 years of development, Pirelli's Cyber Tyre technology is preparing for a wider rollout.
  • That information, combined with software help from Bosch, allows a vehicle to adjust its ABS and traction-control calibrations based on tire data.
  • According to recent reports, "This is one of the worst environments for electronics," explained Pirelli chief technical officer Piero Misani.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After roughly 25 years of development, Pirelli's Cyber Tyre technology is preparing for a wider rollout. The tires use a sensor that looks a lot like a Dexcom G7 to feed temperature, air pressure, acceleration, and identification data to a vehicle's computers.

That information, combined with software help from Bosch, allows a vehicle to adjust its ABS and traction-control calibrations based on tire data. For example, swap your summer tires for squishier winter rubber, and a compatible car could recognize the change and automatically adjust how its electronic controls intervene, leaving you free to imagine a world where maybe we all just drove better.

See all results for used cars for sale near 29405.

According to recent reports, "This is one of the worst environments for electronics," explained Pirelli chief technical officer Piero Misani. The sensor, weighing just 13 grams, is bonded to the tire's inner liner beneath the tread using a specially developed adhesive and rubber housing. The process was developed using learnings from Pirelli's Noise Cancelling System, which uses foam inside the tire to absorb sound waves and reduce cabin vibration. The sensor must survive extreme temperatures, constant flexing, and the insane lateral g-forces that tires are susceptible to at over 200 mph. Engineers explained that its battery is designed to outlast the tire and enters a low-power sleep mode during extended storage.

The more inspiring part is what the car does with the information it gathers. As we found in our recent all-weather tire comparison test, summer, winter, and all-season tires perform dramatically differently. Yet a vehicle's electronic controls are generally calibrated around its original equipment, using things like wheel speed sensors that aren’t as close to the road surface as the Cyber Tyre. Instead, it identifies the specific tire installed at each corner, allowing it to use different wheel-slip targets. And with the sensor attached to the inside of the tire, the data informing those systems is closer to the road surface than ever.

We sampled the technology at Las Vegas Motor Speedway in two Mercedes-AMG GT63 S four-doors wearing Cyber Tyre-equipped P Zero MS all-season tires.

Industry observers note that the first exercise had us pin the throttle through a corner from 40 mph using three different traction-control calibrations, all on the same P Zero MS all-season tires. The first, intended for ultra-high-performance summer tires, was overly restrictive, cutting power before the tires could deliver much acceleration. The second, calibrated for winter tires, permitted considerably more wheelspin, making the AMG easy to slide. Despite that setting being the most fun (and our favorite), Cyber Tyre delivered a happy medium, allowing more controlled acceleration without either extreme.

See all results for used cars for sale near 29405.

Sources indicate that this is where Cyber Tyre begins to make the case against selectable drive modes. The same car, wearing the same tires, just behaved three different ways without any mechanical changes. It's not going to replace the button that stiffens your dampers or changes your exhaust note, but it could eventually make some traction-related settings redundant.

Industry observers note that the second AMG demonstrated ABS braking from 65 mph. With Cyber Tyre integration active, our stopping distance improved by 0.9 meter, or about three feet, according to Pirelli's instrumentation. That's not dramatically different, but still a measurable improvement.

Sources indicate that of course, these demonstrations weren't proof that Cyber Tyre can outperform a conventional system already calibrated for the correct tires. And the technology isn't smart enough to know it's snowing just because the tires are cold. But the distinction is that Cyber Tyre can give the car information about its tires without the driver doing anything. That could be super useful as tires wear, temperatures change, or owners swap between summer and winter sets. Pirelli is also developing tire-wear estimates using its sensor data, which could prove useful for fleet operators managing hundreds of vehicles.

Pirelli and Bosch declared their development partnership in 2024, and the technology has already appeared in vehicles from McLaren and Pagani. Pirelli executives say a substantially higher-volume application should be announced in the first half of 2027, with production expected in 2028. So it's possible this tech could arrive in models as common as a Ford pickup.

Sources indicate that pirelli is also investing approximately $1.2 billion to expand its Rome, Georgia, manufacturing facility, where Cyber Tyre-equipped products will be produced alongside conventional tires. By 2033, the organization expects annual production capacity to reach six million tires and aims to add up to 1000 engineering jobs.

Industry observers note that they also recently confirmed that China's state-owned Sinochem, formerly Pirelli's largest shareholder, reduced its ownership to 13.6 percent in November. The Italian government has restricted Sinochem's influence and specifically prohibited sharing Cyber Tyre data with entities connected to the Chinese government. Following those governance changes, Pirelli received U.S. authorization to market the technology here. Not that anyone was worried about a Pagani Utopia Roadster being a boon of classified information.

According to recent reports, cyber Tyre isn't about to take the Ford Bronco's G.O.A.T. modes out back to shoot them. There are plenty of reasons to let drivers decide how their cars behave. But after experiencing three dramatically different calibrations in the same AMG, it's easy to see why some of those decisions might eventually be better left to the car. Just make sure we’re able to fully disable them.

Industry observers note that austin Irwin has worked for Car and Driver for over 10 years in various roles. He's steadily worked his way from an entry-level data entry position into driving vehicles for photography and video, and is now reviewing and testing cars. What will he do next? Who knows, but he better be fast.

#156715. Here’s How the Porsche 718 Boxster EV’s Fake Flat-Six and PDK Work

Here’s How the Porsche 718 Boxster EV’s Fake Flat-Six and PDK Work

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the upcoming Porsche 718 Boxster EV hops on board the growing simulated-internal-combustion-engine-and-transmission electric car trend.
  • Industry observers note that the system that debuted in the Taycan is still called “E-Shift” here in the Boxster, and you can turn it on or off via a button on the steering wheel.
  • Recent findings suggest that “It was a big discussion in our tech giant,” Lefevre mentioned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the upcoming Porsche 718 Boxster EV hops on board the growing simulated-internal-combustion-engine-and-transmission electric car trend. We just drove a prototype, and while there’s a lot to discuss about the car in general, it’s also worth honing in on the sound aspect. As you might expect, it’s rather pivotal to the experience behind the wheel.

Industry observers note that the system that debuted in the Taycan is still called “E-Shift” here in the Boxster, and you can turn it on or off via a button on the steering wheel. Porsche chose the 3.4-liter naturally aspirated flat-six from the 981-generation Boxster as its muse. It’s a good choice, but also a bit of a surprise considering the spectacular sound out of the 4.0-liter flat-six found in the previous 718 Boxsters. But Porsche has its reasons, as Dr.-Ing. Sebastian Lefevre, team lead advanced driver assistance systems 718, tells us.

Recent findings suggest that “It was a big discussion in our tech giant,” Lefevre mentioned. “From our point of view, the 4.0 engine is a little bit too soft in the sound. In our company, the 981 GTS sound, six-cylinder, was a little bit louder, and it would also feel more popular and familiar with our old customers.”.

Once you hear the sound, there’s a good chance you’ll end up agreeing with Porsche. Lefevre mentioned the possibility of using the four-cylinder from the previous 718, but just as quickly shot the idea down referencing critique of the flat-four’s sound. How it reproduced the engine and exhaust via speakers is similar to how other OEMs with simulated internal combustion engines in EVs do it.

“A lot of microphones outside, inside,” Lefevre said. “And then we measured it all over the complete rpm range. And then we put it here, in this car, and measure it again. With the speakers, which are installed here. We have two.”.

The most controversial speaker is bound to be the exterior-positioned one. More than anything, however, this exterior speaker exists as a sound maker for occupants to enjoy when the roof is off. It tries to emulate a mid-engine powertrain arrangement by way of the sound emanating from behind the driver and passenger; Porsche increases the volume inside the car with the roof removed, too. That’s a neat idea, but one that struggles to work in practice; I could hear some faint backfires on “downshifts” like Porsche’s ICE cars produce, but the experience is far from that of a real exhaust and engine echoing and reverberating off mountainsides or buildings.

Recent findings suggest that mercedes-AMG has the best ICE simulation around right now, with its AMG GT 4-Door Coupe going so far as to induce proper NVH characteristics by using exciters in the seats. The Boxster EV Prototype we drove relies entirely on the speakers to induce its hypnosis. But E-Shift brings a few theatrics to the table.

Industry observers note that when lining up for a launch control start, Porsche pulses the torque of the electric motor to give a sense of an impending launch. It also lets you run the car into “redline,” tossing you forward with brake torque, just as it would in a manually-shifted gas-powered car. That said, Porsche took some liberties with the 8000-rpm redline depicted in this prototype; the 981 Boxster GTS instrument cluster shows a redline of 7600 rpm, so you have an extra 400 fake revs to play with in the EV.

Not as though this extra headroom matters, however, as Porsche chose to not simulate the torque curve of the flat-six. Instead, peak performance from the single electric motor is always available, and the car shuffles through its fake seven gears as speeds rise and fall. How it shifts is dependent on drive mode per usual with Porsche PDKs, and you can choose between manual or automatic shifting. You’ll even hear a tone difference in the engine noise over the speakers depending on whether you’re on- or off-throttle, just as you would were the real 3.4-liter be gulping in air behind your head.

For our full first impressions from behind the wheel of the 718 Boxster EV, make sure you read our prototype drive review.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there’s been a lot of anticipation for Battlefield 6’s version 1.1.3.0 patch. The patch kicks off the third and final phase of the game’s first season, adding some new holiday-themed content. More the new content itself, the update’s biggest additions are almost entirely gameplay-related.

Unfortunately, for as much as the changes in 1.1.3.0 have been well received, the launch has been marred by a series of technical challenges, some of which are a little unusual.

Immediately after patch 1.1.3.0 went live, players on PC started reporting massive stutters that would occur every few seconds. The issue is especially pronounced in Redsec Battle Royale, but much deadlier in traditional multiplayer.

Industry observers note that battlefield Studios quickly acknowledged it, pointing out a workaround that appears to be working for players on Steam. According to those players, going offline on Steam’s friends menu has fixed stuttering for them.

The matter remains for other players on PC, however, and the developer mentioned it’s working on a proper fix.

In a recent development, perhaps the most disrupting problem the patch has caused is one that prevents players from being able to interact with the game’s menu. Tiles become unresponsive, or outright unselectable when you try to hover near them.

Recent findings suggest that ironically, the top set of tiles designed to make it easy for players to promptly jump into the new content has been the most affected. Restarting the game sometimes fixes the issue, and some players report that it only happens upon first launch after installing the update.

Recent findings suggest that but Battlefield Studios later clarified that, unsurprisingly, there’s an actual reason behind the bug. Once again, a fix is being investigated, and the developer will offer an update once some progress has been made.

Recent findings suggest that A little further down the list of importance is an issue that stops players from being able to skip tiers within the upcoming Winter Offensive bonus path in the game’s battle pass. BF Studios took out the feature entirely while it works on a fix, so while you can continue making progress in the bonus path, you won’t be able to skip tiers.

This is all a shame to see. Outside of all the problems, the meat of the new update has been almost universally praised. The visibility improvements, and netcode updates have been celebrated. Many players were also happy to see meaningful updates to footstep audio and overall clarity.

According to recent reports, it’s also unusual for a Battlefield 6 patch to run into so many problems at launch. The sentiment around 1.1.3.0 so far is that it’s the game’s best and worst update yet. Hopefully those issues will be fixed before the development team breaks for the holidays.

#156712. U.S. Loses Measles-Free Status After 26 Years, a Major Public Health Setback

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1330 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

U.S. Loses Measles-Free Status After 26 Years, a Major Public Health Setback

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1330 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, a major public health achievement that was secured 26 years ago.
  • The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the World Health Organization’s (WHO) regional office for the Americas, determined that measles has spread continuously in the U.S.
  • “Losing a measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation,” PAHO’s director, Jarbas Barbosa, MD, MPH, PhD, said in a media briefing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, a major public health achievement that was secured 26 years ago.

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the World Health Organization’s (WHO) regional office for the Americas, determined that measles has spread continuously in the U.S. for more than 12 months. On November 17, PAHO unveiled the end of the country’s measles elimination status, which it has held since 2000.

“Losing a measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation,” PAHO’s director, Jarbas Barbosa, MD, MPH, PhD, said in a media briefing. “It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at risk of a preventable illness, hospitalization, and death.”.

PAHO’s review examined measles spread starting January 20, 2025, when the first person became ill in a large West Texas outbreak, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

CDC data show 5,412 confirmed measles cases this year as of November 12. That’s the highest annual total since 1991 and more than double the 2025 count of 2,289 cases.

Andi Shane, MD, chief of pediatric infectious diseases at Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta, called the U.S. losing measles elimination status “a public health alarm that we are not being effective and we’re not controlling measles as well.”.

The measles virus is highly contagious. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. People can catch it in a room up to two hours after an infected person has left, according to the CDC.

“There’s really been very little measles in the United States over the past 25 years until January 2025,” William Moss, MD, a professor of epidemiology at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, told Healthline.

According to recent reports, losing the status itself doesn’t change much about daily life for most Americans, Moss noted. The concern is the measles outbreaks, hospitalizations and deaths behind the loss, he said.

He called the loss “a major red flag” after “enormous efforts over the past 26 years” to keep the status.

Sources indicate that A country loses its elimination status when there is “uninterrupted circulation of the same virus genotype and lineage for 12 months or more,” according to PAHO. Shane explained it this way: “For the past 12 months in the United States, we’ve had ongoing circulation of the measles virus and person-to-person transmission is occurring.”.

Canada lost its elimination status in November 2025, and the U.K. and five European countries lost theirs earlier in 2026.

The U.S. can regain the status. “Other countries have done that,” Moss noted. Brazil, which lost its status in 2019, regained it in November 2024. Venezuela, which lost its status in 2018, regained it in 2023, according to PAHO.

Recent findings suggest that before the measles vaccine, measles infected an estimated 3 million to 4 million Americans each year, according to the CDC. Among reported cases, about 400 to 500 people died each year, 48,000 needed hospital care, and 1,000 developed encephalitis, or brain swelling.

Here’s a timeline of measles elimination in the U.S.:.

It has been revealed that moss mentioned elimination efforts “really intensified” after a large outbreak from 1989 to 1992. Part of that push was “really promoting school entry vaccination checks,” he said.

“That was one of the key policy changes that I think allowed for measles elimination in the United States.”.

Every state and Washington, D.C., require children to be vaccinated against measles to attend school, though exemptions vary by state, according to the nonprofit health policy organization KFF.

Fewer kindergartners are getting the MMR vaccine, according to the CDC.

Kindergarten MMR coverage fell from 95.2% in the 2019–2020 school year to 92.4% in 2025–2026. About 280,000 kindergartners started the 2025–2026 school year without records showing they had completed the MMR series, the CDC reported.

Shane mentioned “95 out of 100 people need to be protected against measles” for a community to get herd protection.

“So since we’ve been below that for many, many months, that is also contributing to the loss of our elimination status,” she remarked.

Recent findings suggest that “It takes two things to have a measles outbreak,” Moss mentioned. A community needs low vaccine coverage, and someone with measles has to enter it and “start the chain of transmission,” he said.

About 96% of this year’s cases were among people who were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status, up from 93% in 2025, according to the CDC.

Moss noted many of those cases are adults.

“This is particularly true in Pennsylvania, where about two-thirds of the cases are in adults,” he mentioned. Many never got vaccinated as kids and grew up while measles was rare, so they never built natural immunity, he said.

It has been revealed that he noted that having so many unvaccinated adults puts pregnant people and adults with chronic conditions like lung disease at risk of serious illness. The U.S. has already seen “dozens of pregnant women actually getting infected during pregnancy,” he said.Infected parents can also spread measles to young children and grandparents, Shane said. Shane traced much of the hesitancy to the pandemic. “With COVID there’s been an overall distrust in vaccines and vaccination that initially started with COVID but has now spread to other vaccines,” she said.

Moss pointed to the federal government. “We know what it takes to achieve and sustain elimination. We have the expertise. We have the resources,” he said.

He cited staff cuts at the CDC and stated messaging from Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and President Donald Trump has undermined vaccine confidence. He called federal messaging on vaccines “really mixed and weak.”.

Moss also criticized the President’s August 10 executive order calling for the MMR vaccine to be split into separate shots for each disease.

“There’s no justification for that, and those vaccines don’t even exist in the United States,” he noted.

Measles may cause ear infections, diarrhea, pneumonia, encephalitis and, in some cases, death, according to the CDC. The disease may also weaken the immune system for weeks to a year after recovery, raising the risk of flu, COVID-19, or RSV, Shane said. “It’s not a benign childhood disease,” Moss said.

Industry observers note that the best protection against measles is two doses of the MMR vaccine, which are about 97% effective, according to the CDC. Shane remarked, “There are not very many other things we do in life that give you such great protection.” People who missed doses can still catch up, she added. “If you just don’t know or can’t tell, there’s no harm — as long as you’re eligible — in getting another MMR vaccine.”.

Shane added that “parents really want to do the right thing for their children.”.

In a recent development, “We know that the MMR vaccine — that’s the vaccine that provides protection against measles — is a safe vaccine. It’s a very effective vaccine,” Shane mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that babies under 12 months are too young for the vaccine. “So they depend on the protection of the people around them,” Shane remarked.

Recent findings suggest that the CDC recommends a first MMR dose at 12 to 15 months and a second at 4 to 6 years. Babies 6 to 11 months old who will travel internationally should get an early dose, and adults without proof of immunity should get at least one dose, according to the CDC.

To stop the outbreaks, Moss remarked the U.S. will need to “increase vaccine coverage, particularly in those communities that have had long-standing low vaccine rates.”.

Industry observers note that so far, the response has been “more reactive than proactive,” Moss remarked. Public health teams scramble once an outbreak starts, he said, and he wants more outreach to at-risk communities before measles arrives.

“I am worried about the ability of the United States to regain measles elimination status in the current climate,” Moss said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, volkswagen is giving EV drivers in Germany a reason to plug in at home, even if they don’t need a charge. VW’s charging subsidiary, Elli, is launching a vehicle-to-grid (V2G) program in December that pays drivers up to €720 in the first year for keeping a compatible EV plugged in.

The bidirectional home charger costs €1,995, including tax and shipping. Installation is extra.

Elli pays a plug-in bonus of €0.24 for each eligible hour the EV is plugged into the Elli BiDi DC charger. Sessions have to last at least three hours, and drivers need 250 plugged-in hours a month – a little over eight hours a day on average – to earn the full €60 monthly bonus. VW estimates the full first-year bonus could cover the electricity for around 15,500 km (9,600 miles) in an ID.3 Neo Trend, assuming electricity costs €0.33 per kWh.

Recent findings suggest that elli’s “V2G Flow” electricity plan covers the home and the car. Elli expects to offer a separate payment later under its “V2G Return” plan, at €0.40 for each kWh the car sends back to the grid. Drivers use Elli’s app to set when they need the car and how much charge they want by then. The system handles charging and, when available, sends power back to the grid according to that schedule.

The 11 kW DC charger supports 400- and 800-volt EVs, but eligibility depends on the model and which functions VW has enabled. The offer spans Volkswagen, Cupra, Škoda, and Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles; the latter has its own ordering process. Drivers also need a compatible smart meter and must complete Elli’s online site check and obtain an installation quote before they can order the charger.

In a recent development, BMW and E.ON opened orders in Germany for their home V2G package for the iX3 in February. VW is bringing its offer to four brands, and it says around 360,000 of its EVs built on VW Group’s shared electric platform in Germany have the technical groundwork for bidirectional charging. Drivers will still need to check whether their specific EV qualifies.

According to recent reports, elli is working with bidirectional charging company The Mobility House Energy to pool the available battery capacity of participating EVs. It looks to expand V2G to more European markets in 2027 and launch a separate vehicle-to-home (V2H) product that would let households use electricity stored in their EV, including surplus rooftop solar saved for later use.

#156710. The pumpkin’s strange journey from toxic plant to a seasonal staple

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (602 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

The pumpkin’s strange journey from toxic plant to a seasonal staple

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (602 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that from jack-o-lanterns and cute tabletop knickknacks to pumpkin pie and the ever popular pumpkin spice latte, the iconic squash fills every nook and cranny of the fall season.
  • Logan Kistler, an anthropologist at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History, is interested in the origin stories of the crops that feed humanity.
  • In a recent development, it’s worth highlighting that pumpkins are a type of squash.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that from jack-o-lanterns and cute tabletop knickknacks to pumpkin pie and the ever popular pumpkin spice latte, the iconic squash fills every nook and cranny of the fall season. But the vegetable has taken a long and strange journey to become our favorite autumnal symbol.

Logan Kistler, an anthropologist at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History, is interested in the origin stories of the crops that feed humanity. And squashes have a strange one. They evolved in the Americas before corn and beans, and played an crucial role in the start of agriculture in the two continents, he tells Popular Science.

In a recent development, it’s worth highlighting that pumpkins are a type of squash. Indeed, “pumpkin” is not an official botanical term, Kistler points out. Squashes, along with zucchini and some gourds, belong to the genus Cucurbita, which is within the broader family Cucurbitaceae, which includes melons, watermelons, cucumbers, and other kinds of gourds.

In a recent development, “Out of this genus Cucurbita at least six different independent lineages of squashes, pumpkins, gourds, and things like that evolved in several different places in the Americas, more or less simultaneously,” says Kistler. However, “the quirky thing about this genus and about a lot of members of this family is in the wild they are unpalatably nasty. They’re incredibly bitter.”.

According to recent reports, that bitterness comes from high concentrations of cucurbitacins. The compounds are the most bitter natural substances that scientists know of. Humans can’t stomach that level of bitterness, but paleontologists have discovered that mastodons (extinct elephant-like mammals) were eating them 30,000 years ago. And that means disseminating them through their feces.

According to recent reports, today, there is no such megafauna in North America that can withstand wild squashes—they’ve lost their evolutionary partner. Cue humans, whose landscaping-shaping settlements give Cucurbita a new ecological niche to fit into.

It has been revealed that “You can kind of think of it as, they lose their one mutualistic partner and then they can just kind of cozy up into this upcoming disturbed landscape that’s created by humans. But then for that relationship to make any sense, they can’t be unpalatably bitter and they can’t be toxic,” Kistler explains.

It appears that these wild squashes had to make, “that evolutionary concession to soften the rind, become less toxic, more palatable and reap the benefits of the protection and care of human cultivators.”.

It seems to have worked. The genus spread far and wide, and wherever it overlaps with humans, they are making use of it. For example, the pumpkins we use to make jack-o-lanterns every Halloween originated in Mexico approximately 10,000 years ago, and there is evidence of humans domesticating them there very early on.

Sources indicate that ultimately, the transition from extremely bitter mastodon snack to today’s autumnal epitome probably involved both Cucurbita’s natural evolutionary journey as well as human intervention. “I tend to think about domestication as, at least in the early phases, the plant is adapting to life alongside humans and that has benefits to humans,” says Kistler, adding that at some point people will get involved more directly.

Industry observers note that but it doesn’t seem like many of these earliest domestication efforts were carried out with the goal of food production. In Florida, they may have been used as fishnet floats, and in the southwestern United States they were likely put to use as containers.

They were eventually carved and—as we all know—baked into pies.

  • Industry observers note that “Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape, or stayed the same,” Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel noted in a statement.
  • Michel explained that while DART flattened one side of Dimorphos into a massive crater, the rest of the space rock isn’t much different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, after over four years of years of anticipation, the European Space Agency has obtained images detailing the aftermath of NASA’s head-on collision with the asteroid Dimorphos. The photos and scans from ESA’s Hera spacecraft highlight the results of the Double Asteroid Redirection Test’s (DART) intentional run-in with Didymos’ 500-foot-wide moonlet Dimorphos in 2022, revealing a stadium-sized crater, cloud of boulders, and a fresh, erratic orbital path.

Industry observers note that “Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape, or stayed the same,” Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel noted in a statement. “Much to our surprise the answer turns out to be all three at once!”.

Michel explained that while DART flattened one side of Dimorphos into a massive crater, the rest of the space rock isn’t much different. Fields of boulders largely remain where they could be seen in DART’s photos from 2022, although the event did drastically change the binary system’s surroundings.

“Another substantial surprise is that Hera is showing that the asteroids are surrounded by hundreds of orbiting boulders, just a few meters in size,” added mission scientist Michael Kueppers.

Hera employed three instruments during its first observations—a thermal infrared imager to measure surface temperature, a 25-color multispectral imager, and a monochrome camera.

The car-sized probe’s work is only just getting started, too. In December, Hera will ultimately travel to barely eight miles from the asteroids, while obtaining increasingly higher-resolution photos. The spacecraft will then deploy a pair of CubeSats to get even closer to the binary system in January 2027. If all goes as planned, one of those devices will even attempt to land on the surface of Dimorphos. The combined measurements from this phase will help researchers understand the impact’s efficiency and improve future deflection strategies.

Hera’s first images were debuted at the dinosaur hall of the Berlin Natural History Museum—an intentional choice on the team’s part.

According to recent reports, “Sixty-six million years ago, an asteroid impact changed the course of life on Earth,” said Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. “Today, for the first time in history, humanity is validating how to prevent such an event from happening again.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, these days, the average fresh car payment in America is over $800 a month. With a payment like that, the last thing you want is to pay even more to access all of your car’s features. The state of New York is now taking steps to ensure that won’t happen; however, like most things in life, there are exceptions.

In a recent development, on Monday, November 23, Upcoming York governor Kathy Hochul signed legislation restricting automakers and dealers from charging consumers subscription fees to access certain features already installed in their vehicles. Essentially, if the hardware necessary to operate a feature is already installed in the vehicle, and activating that feature doesn't require continued support or expense on the part of the automaker, dealer, or third-party service provider, it cannot be put behind a subscription paywall.

In a recent development, A few years ago, BMW faced backlash in Europe for charging a monthly fee in order to enjoy heated seats. BMW has since backed away from that strategy, and under this newly introduced legislation, that subscription approach would no longer be legal. According to a report by the New York Post, companies that violate this new law will face a $250 fine per subscription.

Recent findings suggest that however, this doesn’t mean that Upcoming Yorkers can wave goodbye to all automotive-related subscription services; automakers can still charge for navigation updates, satellite radio, infotainment services, in-car Wi-Fi, roadside assistance, and certain connected vehicle services. Also, software-dependent driver-assistance and automated driving features like Tesla’s Full Self-Driving and General Motors’s Super Cruise are also exempt, meaning motorists shouldn't expect their hands-free highway driving subscriptions to suddenly become cost-free too.

Automakers and third-party companies have about 90 days to get into compliance before the law takes effect on February 27, 2027. It will be interesting to see if other states will follow Latest York’s lead, but the bigger question is if automakers will simply begin charging more for optional equipment at the time of purchase.
